## [SAMR: Training-Free Partial KV Cache Refresh for Streaming Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31892) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction) introduces a training-free method that refreshes only part of the persistent KV cache in block-causal video diffusion models and reconstructs the rest without additional DiT forward passes. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, it reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% versus dense KV updates while improving final-quarter PSNR by 1.61 dB over token reuse. As distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, the clean KV cache update becomes the dominant runtime bottleneck in streaming video diffusion, so this work targets a real and growing cost for long-video generation. The method is training-free and transfers zero-shot to other frozen models like Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B, making it practical for practitioners deploying causal video DiTs. The key insight is that, after removing rotary position phases, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV at a token's exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV; SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the estimates, and reserves true t=0 refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all via tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On held-out VidProM-16 the PSNR gain is 1.14 dB, and zero-shot transfer to Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B reduces reuse-induced step inflation from 2.47 to 2.30 steps/token with a +0.33 dB late-PSNR improvement.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioning each new block on a persistent key-value (KV) cache that stores clean representations from previous blocks; after each block is denoised, an extra noise-free (t=0) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache. Reusing stale KV shortens this update but corrupts conditioning and inflates later denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) encode position information in attention, and removing their phases allows KV estimates from different positions to be compared and fused.

## [TableRouter: Training-Free Routing for Long-Table QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32006) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TableRouter introduces a training-free framework that analyzes each query and routes it either to a computation route, which derives question-conditioned statistics from the full table, or a coverage route, which retrieves relevant rows and column summaries, then passes the chosen context to a frozen LLM in a single call. Across three LLMs and three large-table benchmarks, it outperforms the strongest of six single-call baselines in all nine settings by 1.2–18.3 accuracy points while using 77–95% fewer estimated FLOPs than truncated-table prompting. This work shows that long-table reasoning depends not only on which rows are retrieved but on how evidence is represented, since explicitly providing computed statistics improved accuracy by up to 40.0 points even when all answer-determining rows were available. The training-free, single-call design with amortized indexing makes it practical for deploying frozen LLMs over large tables without fine-tuning or heavy compute. The gains extend to long tables from databases not used in earlier experiments, where TableRouter achieves 35.8% with Qwen2.5-7B versus 16.4% for the strongest external baseline. A controlled experiment isolates evidence access from evidence use, showing that representation matters independently of retrieval completeness.

State-of-the-art methods like GreedyMini and OptMini optimize a binary order and then lift it to DNA's 4-letter alphabet, which imposes structural constraints. Universal hitting sets (UHS) are sets of k-mers that guarantee hitting every sufficiently long sequence, and smaller UHS prefixes enable lower density.

XMind is a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving agents to 'think twice' by cross-referencing working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The framework retrieves risk capsules by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics, and ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. ## [PoseVLN: Pose-Aware Framework Unifies Geometric State Evolution for VLN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32218) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PoseVLN introduces a pose-aware vision-language navigation framework that jointly predicts the next K navigation actions and a local ΔPose over the same horizon in an episode-relative coordinate frame. The predicted ΔPose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to recursively propagate future pose states, forming a continuous geometric evolution from past memory to future motion. This work shows that explicitly modeling geometric state evolution via camera pose can unify memory, state reasoning, and future prediction, outperforming the strongest baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate on R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits. It could influence future VLN research by establishing pose as a geometric bridge across time, with potential benefits for embodied AI and robotics navigation. PoseVLN uses only single RGB observations, avoiding reliance on depth sensors or additional modalities, and organizes visual memory and current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame. The recursive propagation of predicted pose deltas enables continuous state evolution, though the approach is validated only on simulated indoor environments (R2R-CE and RxR-CE) and remains a single arXiv preprint without community discussion or peer review yet.

## [RLVB Trains AI Agents to Act on Their Beliefs, Not Guess Early](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32884) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), a method that rewards agents for gathering more evidence while multiple answers remain possible and for committing only once the evidence is sufficient. Evaluated on three vision-language benchmarks including the new Pro Worlds puzzle benchmark, RLVB improves base models by 17.1% on average across nine settings. This addresses a common failure mode in long-horizon AI agents—premature commitment or 'laziness'—without relying on reward models or LLM judges, which can be costly and unreliable. The approach could lead to more trustworthy agents that know when to act and when to keep investigating, impacting agent training across domains. RLVB uses the simulator's exact posterior over answers at each step to reward further steps while multiple answers remain and to reward commitment once evidence is sufficient; it never reads the agent's written belief line. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12%, and 74% of episodes on the three benchmarks (vs. 8%, 0.4%, and 36% for the base model), and it outperforms PPO with an LLM-judge process reward by 9.3% while using 1.6× fewer GPU-hours.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses automatically checkable signals instead of learned reward models, and RLVB extends this idea by verifying the agent's belief state via the simulator's posterior.

Testing on tiny MLPs, two public CNN zoos, and a constructed population, the authors find no natural setting eligible, though a self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B followed the rewired function in a constructed setting. This work provides a rigorous methodological framework for evaluating whether LLMs genuinely compute from weights or merely recognize statistical fingerprints, which is crucial for the emerging field of weight-space programming and interpretability. The negative result that no natural setting is eligible highlights significant limitations in current evaluation practices and calls for more controlled benchmarks. C2 preserves the readout's singular values, norms, and entry multiset while changing the function in an exactly recomputable way, and the eligibility protocol requires that a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries already predict the target, that C2 change a property specific to the rewiring, and that the reader's identity be attested. In experiments, invariant baselines were near chance on tiny MLPs, weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution but C2's effect was not specific, and per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Weight-space programming refers to the ability of large language models to directly read, interpret, and even write the weights of other neural networks without gradient descent or training loops. Recent studies have shown that frontier models can predict the outputs of small networks from raw weights, but it is unclear whether they truly compute from the weights or simply recognize patterns (fingerprints) in weight space. Function-preserving controls, such as permuting neurons in a way that leaves the network's function unchanged, cannot distinguish between these two possibilities, motivating the need for a counterfactual like C2 that alters the function in a controlled manner.

## [DAGGER: Deployment-Free Quality Estimation for Generative AI Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31252) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DAGGER introduces a deployment-free framework that models generative AI workflows as graphs to estimate end-to-end quality without exhaustively deploying and profiling every model configuration. It decomposes workflow quality into per-node accuracy and per-edge dependency terms, using a novel analytical formulation and SVD-based matrix completion to estimate quality from sparse observations. This addresses a practical and expensive problem in generative AI workflows—quality estimation without exhaustive deployment—and could significantly reduce the cost of model selection and pipeline evaluation. The graph-based approach is technically interesting and may influence how AI pipelines are evaluated in the future. DAGGER estimates workflow quality with a median error of 6.8 percentage points while reducing profiling cost by 10.2× relative to BenchPress, a state-of-the-art baseline, and selects workflow configurations competitive with LLMSelector. It was evaluated on three generative AI workflows across three datasets.

## [FreDraft: On-policy training directly maximizes accepted length for speculative decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31256) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose FreDraft, an on-policy training method for speculative decoding that directly maximizes the expected accepted length of draft tokens by accounting for first-rejection truncation and using prefix-aware credit assignment. The method analytically marginalizes token-level acceptance rates to reduce gradient variance and redistributes part of the gradient into an explicit penalty for overestimated tokens, achieving faster convergence and improved speedup over baselines. Speculative decoding is a key technique for accelerating LLM inference, and draft model quality directly determines the achievable speedup. FreDraft's direct optimization of accepted length addresses a known bottleneck, potentially enabling faster and more efficient inference across a wide range of LLM deployments. The objective accounts for the fact that once a draft token is rejected, all subsequent tokens are discarded, inducing prefix-aware credit assignment that weights each token by its contribution to acceptance of current and future tokens. Analytical marginalization using the target model's vocabulary distribution reduces gradient variance, and an explicit penalty for overestimated tokens preserves the expected gradient while improving training stability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose multiple tokens, which are then verified in parallel by the target model; accepted tokens are kept, and the process repeats. Traditionally, draft models are trained to align token-level distributions with the target model, but this does not directly optimize the length of the accepted prefix, which is the key factor for speedup. On-policy training refers to training the draft model on samples generated by itself, rather than on fixed data, to better match inference conditions.

## [RECAP: RL Framework Trains LLM Agents to Compact Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31258) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RECAP introduces a reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains an LLM agent's policy and its context-compaction summaries, using a behavior distortion objective that measures divergence between the agent's behavior under compressed versus original histories. Experiments on Qwen3.5-4B show absolute gains of 4.6% on BrowseComp-plus and 4.3% on SWE-bench Verified over task-reward-only RL baselines. Long-horizon agents inevitably hit context limits, and lossy summarization can silently derail later decisions; RECAP makes compaction a learned, behavior-preserving skill rather than a heuristic preprocessing step. This could improve reliability for agentic coding and web-browsing tasks where histories grow large. The gradient of the behavior distortion objective decomposes into two signals: a distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. Ablations confirm that jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior is essential, though results are limited to a 4B model and two benchmarks.

**Background**: Context compaction replaces an agent's growing interaction history with a shorter summary so it can keep working within a fixed context window. Prior work typically uses an LLM to summarize, but such summaries are lossy and can change the agent's future behavior. RECAP treats the summary as part of the policy and trains it with reinforcement learning, using self-distillation to align post-compaction actions with those the agent would have taken given the full history.

A new arXiv paper investigates whether Item Response Theory (IRT) generalizes across languages by fitting 1PL, 2PL, and 3PL models per language on Multilingual GSM and Global MMLU, covering over 100 LLMs and 11 languages. It finds that item difficulty is the most stable parameter across languages, followed by guessing and then discrimination, and that instability can be traced to specific items shifting under translation. This work shows that IRT-based benchmark filtering, widely used for efficient model evaluation in English, may not directly transfer to multilingual settings, which could lead to biased model rankings if applied naively. It highlights the need for parameter-aware and item-aware selection when building multilingual LLM benchmarks, affecting researchers and practitioners who rely on cross-lingual evaluations. The study fits three logistic IRT models (1PL, 2PL, 3PL) per language and uses differential item analysis to identify items whose behavior changes under translation. It cautions that model choice should be validated and individual items screened before assuming cross-lingual generalization of IRT-filtered subsets.

**Background**: Item Response Theory (IRT) is a family of statistical models that estimate the relationship between a test taker's latent ability and the probability of answering an item correctly. The 1PL model (equivalent to the Rasch model) uses only item difficulty, the 2PL adds discrimination, and the 3PL adds a guessing parameter. IRT is increasingly used in AI to select informative benchmark items and reduce evaluation costs, but its application has mostly been limited to monolingual settings. Global MMLU is a multilingual benchmark covering 42 languages, designed to address cultural and linguistic biases in evaluation.

MIMPA requires no direct memory access and works by embedding the payload during a correctly answered task so it is retained in a successful record; the attack is further amplified by malicious triggering and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. ## [New Evaluation Framework Scores Agent Recovery from Timed-Out Tool Writes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31318) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.31318) introduces an executable evaluation that separately records tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects to assess how AI agents recover from timed-out tool writes. In 3,456 model episodes, the original task wording yielded only 39/576 valid recoveries when the initial write was absent, while a combined clarification achieved 576/576. This work highlights that evaluating agents only on whether their goal exists can hide harmful recovery actions, as auditing 12 traces changed apparent completion from 10/12 to 8/12. It provides a measurement design and diagnosis of availability, specification, and contract sensitivity, which is critical for building safer AI agents that use tools in production systems. A further 1,584 episodes tested stronger attacks and separated effect definition from recovery recipe: definition alone yielded 276/288 valid recoveries, recipe alone 288/288, and for Luna malicious text was associated with 11.1 percentage points fewer valid recoveries. A separate Claude Code program added 720 successful episodes across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5 with no observed proposal or effect deviations, though the authors note no demonstrated general defense efficacy.

**Background**: AI agents often use tools that perform writes (e.g., to databases or APIs), and a timed-out write may be absent, committed, or still in flight. A new arXiv paper (2611.31429) identifies cross-session answer disclosure, where learners obtain answers by opening new sessions or rephrasing problems, and proposes a persistent per-learner disclosure ledger that gates replies by matching solution structure and result values. In a 3,000-problem simulation, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94–99.5% of problems. The proposed defense could help preserve the pedagogical value of AI tutors by preventing answer leakage without overly restricting honest learners. ## [Study maps layer-wise representation quality across 25 pretrained models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31496) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale empirical study of 25 pretrained text models across four architectural families and four pretraining strategies, evaluated on 13 datasets, finds that peak probing layers depend systematically on architecture and pretraining strategy rather than being at the final layer. The authors distill these findings into the Stable Geometry Index (SGI), a label-free layer selector that improves Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52 over the last-layer baseline. Practitioners often probe the final layer by default, but this work shows that layer choice can be optimized without labels, potentially improving downstream performance for anyone using frozen foundation models. The SGI framework offers a practical, architecture-aware alternative to supervised layer mixing. SGI combines power-law fit quality, effective-rank capacity, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior in a closed-form, fully label-free selector with no fitted coefficients; across 383 evaluation groups it recovers 40% of the gap to the oracle and outperforms a supervised ELMo-style layer mix on the matched subset. Ablations also show that power-law fit quality, not the exponent's proximity to one, is the stronger predictor of layer quality, reversing a common assumption in the spectral-decay literature.

## [Concept Models Certify Wrong Classes on Unseen Compositions, Paper Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.31627) shows that standard concept bottleneck and concept embedding models certify wrong classes 93-94% of the time on unseen combinations of familiar parts, despite having a correct ontology. The authors propose treating the ontology as an error-detecting code and introduce a minimal reference design, OCVE, which reads each part from a local crop in its own forward pass and certifies 52% of images at 0.4% risk on unseen FunnyBirds classes, versus 14% for mask-pooled features and 33% for full-image part readers. This work exposes a critical failure mode in concept-based interpretability: models can produce concept-based explanations that satisfy the ontology yet are wrong, undermining trust in high-stakes applications. The error-detecting-code framing provides a principled way to make concept-based certificates reliable, which could influence the design of trustworthy AI systems in domains like medical diagnosis and autonomous driving. The paper shows that a joint model trained only on visible parts and gated by a localizer still certifies wrong classes 60% of the time, and that part errors copy co-occurring values more often than chance (cross-concept shortcutting). On CUB, isolated region readers are more accurate than an attribute-prototype model (63.1% vs. 55.3%) and certify unseen species at about 6 points less risk; on real traffic signs, isolated readers lower certified risk from 99.8% to 67%, still far too high, with most remaining errors being misread pictograms.

**Background**: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) are neural networks that first predict a set of human-interpretable concepts and then use those concepts to make a final classification, aiming to provide interpretable explanations. Concept embedding models extend CBMs by learning high-dimensional concept representations to improve accuracy while maintaining interpretability. Compositional generalization—the ability to recognize familiar parts in novel combinations—is a key challenge for these models, as they often fail when test inputs contain unseen attribute combinations. ## [Multilingual compaction erases attribute provenance; training-free repair proposed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31668) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.31668) identifies that compacting multilingual conversation history into notes can erase attribute provenance—such as Spanish adjective gender (agotado vs. agotada)—causing recall of stated attributes to drop from 90% to 34% in QA after eviction. The authors propose a training-free write/verify/read repair that marks unstated attributes with paired forms, rewrites unsupported single forms before eviction, and trusts remaining single forms as stated facts, raising F1 by 9–53 points in QA and 12–40 points in agent handovers across five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models. This work exposes a subtle but consequential failure mode in LLM memory systems: compaction can silently discard information that is grammatically obligatory in one language but optional in another, affecting any multilingual assistant that summarizes and evicts old messages. The training-free repair is directly deployable and relevant to researchers and engineers building long-context memory, agent handover, and multilingual QA pipelines. The repair operates at three stages—writing (marking unstated attributes with paired forms like agotado/a), pre-eviction verification (a likelihood check rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones), and reading (trusting remaining single forms as stated facts)—and is evaluated on five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models. The F1 metric penalizes both false assertion and false discounting of attributes, and gains are reported for both QA and agent handover settings.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Context compaction is a common technique in LLM assistants: older messages are summarized into short notes and the originals are evicted to stay within context windows and reduce prefill cost. In multilingual settings, the note's language may require grammatical distinctions that English leaves open—such as Spanish adjective gender—so messages that omit or explicitly state an attribute can produce the same note, making them indistinguishable after eviction. This paper formalizes that provenance loss and proposes a training-free repair across writing, verification, and reading.

CATWAY introduces a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate that uses calibrated language-model confidence to let robot agents decide whether to execute, question, or refuse an instruction. Its thresholds are derived from a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) and it was fitted on household instructions then frozen and tested in-domain, in two new robot domains, and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. This work addresses a critical safety gap in language-model robot agents: unsafe execution costs far more than an unnecessary question, yet prior gates did not derive thresholds from error costs or act on calibrated probabilities. By showing significant cost reductions and zero unsafe executions across domains, CATWAY offers a principled, transferable approach to AI safety in robotics. CATWAY fuses a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility, and risk via logistic regression to estimate probabilities. At eleven generations per decision, it was significantly cheaper than baselines in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 vs. 0.57–0.83), in 9 of 18 in new domains, and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV, and it executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions.

## [Paper Defines 19 Measures to Quantify Proof Dissimilarity in Lean/Mathlib](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31811) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.31811) introduces 19 dissimilarity measures across 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties to quantify how different two proofs of the same theorem are. The authors validate these measures in a Curry-Howard kernel with 5 machine-checked proofs of the infinitude of primes and replicate the analysis in Lean 4/Mathlib with 3 theorems, 19 proofs, and 18 measures. As AI systems generate research-level proofs faster than humans can review them, measuring proof dissimilarity is crucial for detecting duplicated proofs, assessing the diversity of generated proofs, and interpreting AI proofs relative to human mathematics. This framework provides a systematic way to evaluate machine-generated mathematics beyond mere verification. In the Curry-Howard kernel, dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), while semantic measures invert it because Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. The Lean 4/Mathlib replication shows that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs.

## [JECT: Dual-role radiology reports fix context shortcut in chest CT self-supervised learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31849) ⭐️ 7.0/10

JECT introduces a method to overcome the 'context shortcut' in joint-embedding predictive learning for chest CT by using radiology reports both as a condition for the predictor and as a target for the encoder via masked section-text prediction. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, it matches current CT foundation models in classification, retrieval, and nodule malignancy, and task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. This work addresses a fundamental flaw in predictive self-supervised learning where clinically important but unpredictable findings (like small nodules) are ignored because the model learns to predict normal anatomy. The insight that predictive architectures can shortcut around unpredictable findings is broadly relevant beyond chest CT to other medical imaging domains and self-supervised learning in general. Ablations show that the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder itself; however, the conditioned predictor can be reused without extra training to localize where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. The hierarchical 3D encoder predicts at every stage to retain clinical content at every scale, and code and pretrained weights are available.

## [CALVIN-MAX benchmark isolates timing effects of mid-execution changes on robot policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31868) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CALVIN-MAX introduces a 7,828-case benchmark on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, where each case includes one change to objects, camera, robot, or instruction. Each case compares three runs—no change, change from the start of the affected instruction, and change arriving mid-motion—to separately measure the cost of the changed world and the effect of encountering it mid-execution. This benchmark disentangles a previously conflated factor in robot policy robustness: whether a change hurts because the world is different or because it arrives mid-motion. It provides a controlled testbed for embodied AI researchers to diagnose and improve policy robustness to dynamic perturbations. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, ten released policies lose 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction; a change altering what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, while scene or robot changes show no detectable timing effect. The cost persists: policies completing the affected instruction are 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

**Background**: CALVIN (Composing Actions from Language and Vision) is an open-source simulated benchmark for long-horizon language-conditioned robot manipulation, where policies must follow sequences of natural language instructions. Researchers propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm that removes backdoor triggers and stale transitions from latent world models using only cached pretraining moments. A new arXiv paper (2611.32013) analyzes the bias-variance tradeoff between critic-based PPO and critic-free GRPO in reinforcement learning for large language models, showing that the optimal choice depends on batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. This work provides a theoretical framework for choosing between PPO and GRPO, which is crucial as LLMs tackle longer and more complex tasks. It helps researchers and practitioners allocate training compute more effectively, showing that critics pay off at small budgets but their returns diminish at larger budgets. The paper measures how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows, under a shared actor objective. It compares GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents, finding that at longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a popular reinforcement learning algorithm that uses an actor to choose actions and a critic to evaluate them, reducing the variance of policy gradients. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and instead compares multiple answers generated for the same prompt, rewarding answers that beat the group average, which avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. The bias-variance tradeoff is a central concept in machine learning and reinforcement learning, where Monte Carlo methods are unbiased but high variance, while temporal difference methods with bootstrapping introduce bias but reduce variance.

## [Online tuning of Resilience4j policies can backfire without safeguards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32015) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AdaptR4j, a system that uses contextual bandits to dynamically select Resilience4j CircuitBreaker, Retry, and Bulkhead configurations in Spring Boot 3 microservices, was evaluated in a new arXiv preprint. The naive online learning approach performed worse than static defaults in three of four fault scenarios, but adding a safe policy menu and safe exploration with bounded rewards allowed it to outperform defaults in all winnable scenarios (p < 0.001) and cut user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared to the naive design. This work shows that naively applying online learning to resilience policy tuning can degrade performance, highlighting the need for safety constraints in adaptive microservice systems. It provides practical guidance for practitioners and researchers aiming to automate reliability tuning without risking outages. The safeguards—a safe policy menu that excludes circuit breakers stricter than the latency SLO and safe exploration with a bounded reward—were found to carry most of the benefit, as a context-free bandit on the same safe menu performed statistically indistinguishably. The paper also reports a measurement pitfall where a unit mismatch made circuit breakers 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to metrics, causing 94% of user requests to fail while latency and error metrics looked excellent.

## [HuluOPD Distills Five Medical Specialist VLMs into One Lightweight Model Without Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32021) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HuluOPD introduces an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies five heterogeneous medical vision-language specialists (ultrasound, pathology, OCT, fundus photography, dental imaging) into a single lightweight model using only unlabeled prompts, without access to the specialists' training data or reference answers. A continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss enables supervision across differing architectures and tokenizers, and the resulting model with 10% of the combined parameters retains 94% of the specialists' QA performance (89% at 2%). This addresses a real deployment bottleneck in medical AI: specialist models are often private, architecturally incompatible, and costly to run separately. By showing that heterogeneous specialists can be unified without their training data, HuluOPD offers a practical path to lightweight, multi-modality clinical deployment and could lower barriers for hospitals adopting medical VLMs. The method builds HuluOPDCorpus (914k unlabeled prompts) and HuluOPDBench (47k held-out test items) from over 90 public datasets, and evaluates all models under one protocol on 132k test items including third-party benchmarks. The cross-tokenizer loss aligns teacher and student token sequences via continuation matching, but the approach is specialized to medical QA and its generalization to other domains remains untested.

## [ReCast: Making Occupancy World Models Follow Counterfactual Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32029) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces ReCast, an ego-trajectory-guided transformer that grounds future prediction in action-induced geometric correspondence across ego-centric frames, and a new counterfactual action-faithfulness benchmark covering in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories. On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast achieves competitive standard forecasting performance while improving counterfactual forecasting, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution trajectories. Occupancy world models are increasingly used for autonomous driving planning and simulation, but if they ignore the specified ego action, they cannot reliably evaluate counterfactual safety scenarios. This work exposes that flaw and provides both a fix and a benchmark, which could improve the trustworthiness of action-conditioned world models. ReCast decouples historical encoding from future decoding and aligns deformable interactions using relative ego transformations, while retaining flexibility for non-rigid scene evolution. The benchmark explicitly tests in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories, and the gains are most pronounced for out-of-distribution cases.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Occupancy world models predict future 3D scenes conditioned on ego actions, typically by forecasting 3D occupancy grids from past observations. Because driving datasets provide sparse coverage of alternative trajectories for each scene, existing models learn the spatial effect of ego motion implicitly from observed scene-trajectory combinations, which may entangle action effects with scene-trajectory correlations. This makes it unclear whether the model truly follows a given action or merely reproduces correlations seen in training data.

## [PIEQ: Execution-Bound Certification for Safe LLM Agent Infrastructure Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32032) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2611.32032) introduces Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), a certification layer that keeps LLMs outside the trusted computing base and gates infrastructure mutations through provenance isolation, safety shielding, and concurrency governance. PIEQ achieves zero unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits across formal guarantees, etcd fault suites, and live model runs. As LLM-based agents increasingly manage production infrastructure, ensuring their outputs are physically validated before executing changes is critical for safety. PIEQ's approach converts occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions, potentially enabling safer autonomous remediation in critical systems. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance; it binds admission certificates to target execution via snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, and capability-tiered enforcement. However, all benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion and multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as agents to diagnose and remediate incidents in production infrastructure, but their outputs can be unreliable due to shared pretraining biases and correlated errors in ensembles. A trusted computing base (TCB) is the set of components critical to system security; keeping LLMs outside it ensures their failures cannot compromise safety. Assumption-based truth maintenance (ATMS) allows reasoning with multiple simultaneous assumption sets, and linearizability is a strong correctness condition for concurrent systems. PIEQ combines these concepts to certify infrastructure changes only when they are physically justified.

## [Spec-CoFrGeNet stabilizes continued fraction networks via spectral reparametrization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32041) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Spec-CoFrGeNet introduces a novel transformation of partial denominators in continued fraction networks, inspired by Green's functions, to constrain the spectrum of the tridiagonal Hamiltonian, thereby improving training stability and eliminating the need for incremental training. The method achieves performance comparable to standard FFN-based architectures with ~30-50% parameter savings across models like GPT-2 XL, Llama-MoE, and Granite, and also works for image generative modeling with diffusion objectives. This work addresses a key instability in continued fraction networks, making them more practical for large-scale LLM training without complex incremental training procedures. It could enable more parameter-efficient architectures for both language and image generative modeling, reducing computational costs. The reparametrization constrains the spectrum of the tridiagonal Hamiltonian associated with the continued fraction, avoiding poles when denominators approach zero. Experiments show it often outperforms the incremental training baseline and, for the first time, demonstrates effectiveness of continued fraction networks in diffusion-based image generation on a Diffusion Transformer with ~30% parameter savings.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Continued fractions are mathematical expressions that can represent rational functions and have been used to build parameter-efficient neural networks. However, their rational form introduces poles (singularities) when denominators approach zero, causing training instability. Prior work avoided this by enforcing a small positive lower bound on denominators and using incremental training, but performance is sensitive to this bound. Green's functions are mathematical tools from physics that describe responses to point sources and are related to tridiagonal matrices.

## [Integral DeltaNet adds adaptive dual-state memory to linear attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32063) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Integral DeltaNet introduces a dual recurrent state consisting of a fast-updating delta state and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state, with an adaptive readout that combines them across timescales. The authors derive a chunkwise parallel training formulation and evaluate 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Memory collisions are a core bottleneck for fixed-state linear attention in long-context modeling, so a principled dual-state mechanism that improves retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation could inform future efficient LLM architectures. The results are relevant to researchers and engineers working on linear attention, state-space models, and long-context language models. The paper reports comparisons with strong recurrent baselines across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation, and also compares training throughput, activation memory, decoding latency, and memory. As an arXiv preprint without community discussion or independent validation yet, its claims should be treated as preliminary.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Softmax attention compares every token with every previous token, so its key-value cache grows with context length. Linear attention replaces this with a linear formulation that compresses past information into a fixed-size recurrent state, enabling linear-time computation but causing memory collisions when different past items overwrite each other. DeltaNet mitigates this with delta-rule updates that correct the state by prediction error, and Gated DeltaNet adds gating, but these mechanisms can also discard information useful for future predictions.

## [MARGIN: Risk-Aware Agent Refines Robot Programs via Near-Miss Margin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32093) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MARGIN introduces a near-miss margin signal, defined as the fraction of execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout, to prioritize fragile robot programs and guide repairs. Evaluated on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite, it reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0% across two rounds on 37 LIBERO-Pro tasks, with 18.0-20.0% reductions on the other benchmarks. Binary success metrics saturate even when robot programs remain fragile on unseen scenes, so this risk-aware signal offers a practical way to select revisions that increase execution headroom and generalize better. The approach could improve the reliability and efficiency of robot-programming agents in real-world deployment where hidden failures are costly. The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774, and low-margin programs show 2.97 times higher failure risk; an exact safe-racing rule cuts candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while preserving identical selections. Paired execution probes further improve acceptance decisions by catching hidden regressions.

Researchers introduced Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated hospital-environment benchmark with 3,368 questions across eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts, and found that the best open and proprietary multimodal LLMs reach only 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, versus 79.0% for physicians on a subset. ## [RetraQ: Manifold-Constrained Critic Guidance for Flow Policies in RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32148) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RetraQ introduces a manifold-constrained critic guidance method that uses the geometry of a pretrained flow-matching policy to filter critic gradients and retract actions onto the behavior manifold, improving policy optimization. In experiments, test-time RetraQ raised the success rate of a behavior-cloned π0.5 policy from 55.0% to 76.7% on a real-world plug-insertion task, and online training further increased success to 98.3% in 30 minutes and 100% within one hour. This work addresses a known problem in reinforcement learning with generative policies: critic extrapolation errors can mislead action gradients even when the critic fits the behavior data well. By constraining guidance to the data-supported manifold, RetraQ improves stability and final performance, which could benefit robotics and other domains where offline-to-online RL with flow-matching policies is used. RetraQ uses a single velocity evaluation of the frozen flow to define a denoising map, then filters the critic gradient with the map's Jacobian and applies the map itself to correct the updated action. The analysis characterizes when these operations approximate tangent filtering and retraction onto the behavior manifold, and the same update guides actions at test time and provides targets for policy distillation and online RL.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Flow matching is a generative modeling paradigm that trains continuous normalizing flows by matching a vector field to a target velocity field, enabling efficient sampling. In reinforcement learning, a critic can guide a pretrained policy by steering actions toward higher predicted value, but gradients pointing away from the data distribution can exploit critic errors. Manifold constraints restrict updates to a data-supported region, and RetraQ combines these ideas by using the flow's geometry to keep guided actions on the behavior manifold.

## [STEP-GRM supervises intermediate evaluation steps in generative reward models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32161) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces STEP-GRM, a framework that directly supervises the intermediate evaluation process of rubric-based generative reward models (GRMs) by providing structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, in addition to conventional preference supervision. Experiments show that STEP-GRM achieves strong performance on standard reward-modeling benchmarks while improving the consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations. This work addresses a key limitation in generative reward models: under outcome-only supervision, models may produce correct final preferences through weak or unsupported intermediate judgments, essentially post-hoc rationalization. By ensuring more reliable evaluation processes, STEP-GRM's reward signals also lead to better downstream policy optimization, showing practical gains beyond reward-model accuracy. STEP-GRM provides structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, encouraging the model to learn not only the correct final preference but also a more reliable process for reaching it. The approach is evaluated on standard reward-modeling benchmarks and demonstrates improved consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations.

## [RightDiff: Generative Reward Models Judge by Contrastive Differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32166) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RightDiff proposes a generative reward model that structures pairwise evaluation into a single autoregressive trajectory: it discovers contrastive differences between candidate responses, categorizes them as material or immaterial, and induces pair-specific rubrics before adjudication. It is trained with a difference-alignment reward regularized by budget-constrained one-to-one matching and multiplicative gating, achieving state-of-the-art results on RewardBench and RM-Bench. This work addresses two known weaknesses of generative reward models—generic query-level rubrics and rationale drift toward superficial shortcuts like verbosity—which are critical for reliable RLHF and LLM alignment. By surpassing open-source reward models and proprietary LLM judges, RightDiff could improve downstream preference optimization such as DPO on Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval. RightDiff synthesizes demonstration data via response-isolated prompts to avoid post-hoc rationalization, and its difference-alignment reward uses budget-constrained one-to-one matching and multiplicative gating to prevent rationale drift. It effectively resists length shortcuts while providing reliable supervision for direct preference optimization.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Generative reward models (GenRM) use next-token prediction to evaluate outputs, integrating generation and verification within a single model, and are widely used in RLHF to align LLMs with human preferences. Pairwise preference evaluation asks a judge to compare two responses, but models often exploit superficial cues like verbosity or formatting, a phenomenon known as rationale drift, where the stated reasoning diverges from the actual decision basis.

## [Protein structure tokenizers benchmarked for generation 'writability'](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32168) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper benchmarks eight protein structure tokenizers by training an identical 9B language model to generate structure tokens, measuring 'writability' across 96 experimental cells. Final TM-scores range from 0.662 to 0.378 under identical conditions, and neither codebook size nor reconstruction fidelity explains the spread. This work introduces 'writability' as a distinct criterion for selecting protein structure tokenizers, showing that tokenizers chosen for reconstruction accuracy may not be optimal for generative modeling. It could influence how protein ML researchers design and select tokenizers for structure-based language models. The study finds that local structure preservation of the code space explains writability differences: in DPLM-2, a one-bit codeword error costs only 0.019 TM versus 0.347 for a random codeword, while FoldToken4 fails both tests at the same codebook size. Controls show a noise floor of σ=0.0067 TM, a near-orthogonal relationship between a reference-free geometry panel and TM (Pearson -0.58), and null results for two pre-registered interventions due to saturation at 1.5B tokens.

**Background**: Protein structure tokenizers convert continuous 3D structures into discrete tokens that language models can process, similar to how text tokenizers work. TM-score is a standard metric for structural similarity, where a score above 0.5 generally indicates a correctly folded protein.

## [Frequency Band in Geometric RoPE Can Reverse Benchmark Rankings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32171) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.32171) shows that the frequency band in geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) is an unstandardized but critical hyperparameter. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline with 144-channel heads (47M model) but trails by 1.2 dB with 48-channel heads (25M model), and populating a 243x frequency range with four frequencies instead of the default 3x recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. This work reveals that an overlooked hyperparameter can reverse benchmark rankings, meaning prior comparisons of multi-view attention methods may be confounded by inconsistent frequency band settings. It advocates for reporting and matching frequency bands in future benchmarks, which could lead to fairer evaluations and improved performance in 3D-aware transformers. The paper finds that overly narrow bands blur correspondence, while overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE due to a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass but leaves their gradients undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90–93% of the lost PSNR, and the authors distill practical guidelines such as setting bands in image coordinates and avoiding unconditional same-view damping.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Rotary position encodings (RoPE) encode token positions by rotating features with rotation matrices, and are widely used in modern transformers. Geometric RoPE extends this to multi-view attention by incorporating 3D camera geometry—rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies (its frequency band), but existing implementations inherit defaults from standard 2D RoPE without standardization. RayRoPE is a specific geometric RoPE method for multi-view attention, and RealEstate10K is a benchmark dataset for novel view synthesis.

## [Mock Jurors Blame AI but Fault Leaks to Victims, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32188) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A pre-registered experiment with 199 U.S. mock jurors found that 36% blame the generative AI system itself for harm, and this blame often 'leaks' to the victim or AI user in 27% to 73% of AI-blaming cases. The study also examined how discontinuous liability doctrines like contributory negligence and joint and several liability influence fault allocation. This research reveals a potential bias in how juries assign fault in AI-related tort cases, which could unfairly reduce compensation for victims and complicate liability frameworks as generative AI becomes more prevalent. It suggests that a narrow joint and several liability exception for AI deployers might mitigate these effects without increasing jury nullification risks. The experiment used Prolific participants and focused on U.S. tort doctrines with fault-percentage thresholds (50% or 51% cliffs). Notably, mock jurors rarely changed blame assignment across the liability cliff, but they did not acknowledge the legal doctrine or its monetary consequences when explaining their decisions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Tort law assigns liability for harm, and generative AI complicates this because the AI itself cannot be held legally responsible. Contributory negligence bars recovery if the plaintiff is also negligent, while joint and several liability allows plaintiffs to recover full damages from any liable defendant. Discontinuous doctrines create 'cliffs' where compensation jumps to zero or full damages based on fault percentages.

## [Alpha-fair framework unifies multi-label feature selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32200) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes FLIC, an α-fair welfare framework for multi-label feature selection that treats labels as agents and greedily maximizes the α-fair welfare of per-label information coverage. A single parameter α spans utilitarian (α=0), proportionally fair (α=1), and max-min (α→∞) selection, subsuming a dozen published relevance terms as special cases, approximations, or limits. This work provides a unified theoretical foundation for multi-label feature selection, showing that existing information-theoretic filters are implicit social welfare functions. It enables principled selection of fairness levels via α and offers strong approximation guarantees, impacting researchers in machine learning and information theory. The objective is monotone submodular for α≥0, yielding a (1-1/e)-approximation via greedy selection, but fails for α<0 and the max-min limit is inapproximable. FLIC uses bias-corrected, label-wise conditional information without a relevance-redundancy trade-off parameter, and on 22 datasets it outperforms 14 filters on most metrics.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Multi-label feature selection aims to choose a subset of features that are relevant to multiple labels simultaneously, a common task in high-dimensional data analysis. Information-theoretic filters score features by their mutual information with labels, but existing methods differ in how they distribute relevance across labels. The α-fair welfare function, originating from resource allocation, balances efficiency and fairness by varying a single parameter α. Submodular optimization provides greedy algorithms with approximation guarantees for maximizing monotone submodular functions.

## [Tencent's OmniEVIE: 4.5B multi-vector embedding for unified multimodal retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32203) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Tencent researchers released OmniEVIE, a 4.5B-parameter multi-vector embedding model that covers text, images, visual documents, video, and tools with a single compressed index and a three-stage retriever. Each record stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 (9,472 bytes, or 8.82 GiB per million records), enabling coarse, middle, and final search while localizing hits to page regions or video intervals. The model addresses real serving-cost and localization problems in multimodal retrieval, where single-vector embeddings lose local evidence and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. Its reported speedups (11.1x and 25.3x faster than exact 4096-d single-vector search on 1M and 5M records) could make large-scale multimodal search practical for production systems. OmniEVIE scores 60.68 (full d=2048 sequence) and 60.06 (K128 x d64 int8 index) on MMEB-V3 (190 tasks), 77.96 on MMEB-V2, and 62.96 on ViDoRe V3; on QVHighlights, the peak falls inside the labeled segment for 78.0% of queries and the returned span intersects it for 94.3% versus 44.9% random. Training, merging, indexing, and retrieval are co-designed with a three-grade evidence check, dynamic sampling, ST-HAC compression during training, parameter-block merging, and a saliency gate with a noise floor.

OmniEVIE builds on this trade-off by co-designing a compressed multi-vector index with the embedding model itself.

## [RoboClock: A New Benchmark for Time-Aware Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32233) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RoboClock introduces a unified benchmark of 60 tasks across five application domains to evaluate time-aware robotic manipulation under three types of temporal constraints: Temporal Window, Event-Reactive, and Throughput. It also proposes a Latency-Aligned evaluation protocol that advances environment time during model inference and control delays, and reports that the best method, a trained VLA, achieves only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy tasks. Existing robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize spatial correctness and logical task completion, overlooking temporal constraints that are critical in real-world applications. RoboClock fills this gap by providing a structured taxonomy and latency-aligned metrics, which could drive joint optimization of physical competence, temporal reasoning, and execution latency in embodied AI systems. The benchmark evaluates over 30 methods and reveals persistent challenges in generalization and transfer, with the best VLA achieving only 8.3% temporal success on Easy-level tasks. The Latency-Aligned protocol continuously advances environment time during inference and control-interface delays, paired with time-sensitive metrics to capture temporal failures.

**Background**: Robotic manipulation benchmarks typically assess whether a robot can grasp, move, or assemble objects correctly in space, but they often ignore timing. In real-world settings, a robot may fail if it acts outside a valid time window, responds too slowly to an event, or cannot meet required throughput. RoboClock addresses this by structuring tasks around temporal constraints and introducing a latency-aware evaluation protocol, drawing on concepts like temporal logic and spatio-temporal constraints from robotics planning.

## [Boundary-Aware Policy Learning Improves Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32238) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, a two-stage method that first shapes a wide, well-defined handoff boundary for a visuomotor policy via Boundary-Explicit Training on contact segments with diverse start poses, then expands it through Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement on curated successful rollouts. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, the system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes while cutting API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%. This work addresses a concrete failure mode in agent-orchestrated robot systems—the handoff moment when a multimodal agent invokes a visuomotor policy outside its reliable start-state region—and shows that explicitly shaping the boundary between agent and policy yields large gains in success, cost, and speed. It suggests that robust embodied AI orchestration depends not only on improving individual components but also on managing the interface between them. The method relies on a simple handoff protocol to communicate the policy's boundary to the agent, and the self-improvement stage extends the boundary toward earlier task stages so the agent can hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Evaluation is limited to simulated benchmarks (RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo), and the approach assumes access to contact segments and curated successful rollouts for training.

## [DAiSy: Lightweight Linear Model for Online Data Selection in LLM Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32294) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DAiSy introduces a lightweight linear auxiliary model that predicts data utility scores from frozen document embeddings, eliminating the need for full forward-backward passes on every candidate document during online data selection for LLM pretraining. The linear estimator is updated alongside the main language model to fit the exact gradient-based utility scores obtained from regular training steps, and experiments show consistent improvements in English and multilingual pretraining that survive instruction tuning. This work addresses a key inefficiency in model-aware online data selection, where scoring a document costs as much as training on it, by reducing scoring to a simple linear transformation. It could make online data selection practical at scale for LLM pretraining, lowering compute and infrastructure burdens for researchers and practitioners. The linear estimator is trained to match gradient-based utility scores from the backward pass of regular training steps, so scoring a candidate requires only a linear transformation over frozen embeddings. The method is evaluated for LLM pretraining in English and multilingual scenarios with various steering target designs, and the gains consistently survive the instruction-tuning phase.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Online data selection for LLM pretraining aims to prioritize training documents that are most useful given the model's current state, often by ranking candidates using gradient-based data utility scores. However, computing these scores requires a full forward-backward pass of the main model on every candidate, which is as expensive as training on that document. DAiSy avoids this by learning a lightweight linear model that predicts utility scores from frozen document embeddings, which are fixed representations of text produced by a pretrained model.

## [QGVM Minimizes Images Sent to Cloud VLMs to Reduce Privacy Leakage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32302) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced QGVM, a framework that locally minimizes images before sending them to cloud vision-language models by preserving only query-relevant content and suppressing unnecessary sensitive information. Evaluated with OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol, QGVM achieved 85.3% answer correctness on DoxBench versus 77.5% for PGP, while reducing geolocation attacker success within 1 km to 5.8% from 25.7% on unprotected images. This work addresses a core privacy risk in cloud-based multimodal AI: users must send full images beyond their trust boundary even when the query needs only a small part. By showing that query-guided minimization can improve both utility and privacy over prior methods, it offers a practical path for safer use of cloud VLMs in sensitive applications. QGVM combines query grounding with an independent sensitive-item inventory to decide disclosure necessity at the type, instance, and text-content levels, then renders a minimized image for a black-box downstream VLM. On Scene-Privacy it cut face re-identification from 27.7% (PGP) to 4.5%, and on BIV-Priv-Seg it reduced unnecessary private-text recovery from 33.9% to 15.3%; paired-query tests showed 69.6% correct disclosure switching versus 29.1% for grounding-only cropping.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Cloud vision-language models process images on remote servers, so any image sent leaves the user's local trust boundary and may expose sensitive details the query does not require. Prior privacy approaches often use query-agnostic anonymization, which can remove information that is actually needed or fail to suppress content that is not. QGVM instead distinguishes visual relevance from disclosure necessity, preserving sensitive content only when the query explicitly requires it.

## [ASTERISM audit reveals single-image shortcut in multimodal benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32316) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An audit of 19 public multi-image MLLM benchmarks covering about 33k items found that 24.2% can be answered from a single image or the question alone, a phenomenon the authors call the single-image shortcut. They release ASTERISM, an 18.7k-item audited benchmark (2.0k items corrected or rewritten) that requires multiple images, along with ASTERISM-Train (49k items) and ASTERISM-Lite, a manually verified hard subset. The finding suggests that many multi-image benchmarks may be measuring single-image recognition rather than cross-image reasoning, potentially inflating reported MLLM capabilities. ASTERISM provides a cleaner evaluation target and the proposed CICA training method addresses the shortcut at training time, which could affect how future multimodal models are evaluated and post-trained. On shortcut items, MLLMs recover a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over text alone, and they still take the shortcut on items where one image is insufficient, repeating single-image answers at above-chance rates. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores only 68%, and existing RLVR objectives add little; the proposed cross-image credit assignment (CICA) raises ASTERISM scores by 2.6 to 6.0 points on three open-source MLLMs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) combine a language model with vision encoders to process both text and images. Multi-image benchmarks are designed to test whether a model can integrate evidence across several images, but if individual items can be solved from one image, the benchmark fails to isolate that skill. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a common post-training technique that rewards correct final answers, which can inadvertently reinforce shortcut behavior when a single image suffices.

## [Top-K Token Selection in LLM Attention Is Provably Suboptimal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32324) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proves that selecting top-K tokens by individual importance scores is insufficient for optimal attention, with an unbounded multiplicative gap in KL divergence and empirical audits on SmolLM2, Gemma, and Qwen showing that exact-singleton Top-4 leaves at least 10% relative improvement in 55/60, 49/60, and 60/60 cases, respectively. This challenges the widely used top-K sparse attention strategy in long-context LLMs, showing that joint support quality matters and motivating downstream-aware selection methods that could improve efficiency and accuracy of inference under memory constraints. The paper constructs a four-position example where the ranked pair incurs 133.2 times the KL divergence of the optimal pair, proves the gap is unbounded, and introduces SwapCert, a same-budget one-swap audit that detects 157/164 improving cases; a KL-margin certificate links support fidelity to next-token stability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Long-context language models often use sparse attention to reduce computation, keeping only a subset of past tokens (top-K) for each query based on individual importance scores. However, attention weights are renormalized over the selected set, so the best individual tokens may not form the best combination. This paper investigates whether independent ranking suffices even when scores exactly measure the downstream effect of deleting each token.

## [DiCT: X-ray VLMs Learn 3D Reasoning via CT Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32344) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose DiCT, a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that uses a CT vision-language model to guide an X-ray VLM, enabling it to perform 3D spatial reasoning directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference. Experiments on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA show a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77× lower inference computation. This work addresses a fundamental limitation of X-ray diagnosis—the loss of 3D spatial information in 2D projections—by transferring 3D anatomical knowledge from CT to X-ray VLMs, potentially improving radiological reasoning without the cost and radiation of CT scans. It could impact clinical workflows by enabling more accurate abnormality localization and spatial relationship assessment from standard X-rays. The framework consists of three stages: instruct the dreamer (equipping the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning and a structured interface distinguishing X-ray observations from CT imagination), visualize the dream (CT-guided on-policy distillation where the CT teacher selectively guides the student's reasoning trajectories), and manifest the dream (adapting reasoning from digitally reconstructed radiographs to real clinical X-rays). The method is evaluated across two VLM backbones, and code is available on GitHub.

## [Gradient alignment beats test-time gains for self-distillation, paper finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32390) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.32390) systematically analyzes mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models and finds that gradient-based alignment, rather than immediate test-time performance improvement, is a more reliable indicator of downstream distillation gains. Based on this, the authors propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their estimated training utility. The finding could lead to more stable and effective self-evolving LLM pipelines that avoid degrading model parameters through misguided distillation. The paper evaluates diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning by selecting experiences based on estimated training utility rather than test-time success. The abstract does not specify model sizes or benchmark names, and no community discussion is available to validate impact.

Researchers introduced CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems derived from six real CPUs, spanning small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and covering SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 on CPU-Eval is 45.14 percentage points lower than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL. ## [Time-horizon curves mask within-task hazards; repeated runs can identify them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32415) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2611.32415) shows that log-logistic time-horizon curves used to evaluate AI agents are mixtures of constant-hazard curves, so they cannot support conclusions that failure hazard declines within a task. The paper proposes using repeated runs of the same task to restore identification of within-task hazard trends under a Weibull frailty model, and applies the method to METR's public run-level data. This work challenges a common methodology in AI agent evaluation, showing that widely used time-horizon curves can obscure within-task hazard trends and lead to incorrect conclusions about agent reliability. It has important implications for how researchers and practitioners assess and compare AI agents, especially as agents are deployed on longer, multi-step tasks. The paper proves that every log-logistic horizon curve with slope β≤1 is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve arises from any within-task Weibull shape k≥β. On METR's public data, under assumptions the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for 1/k lies entirely above one, and for five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one, rejecting a non-increasing average hazard under a log-logistic cross-section.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Time-horizon curves plot an AI agent's success probability against the human time needed for a task, and recent analyses fit survival models to these curves to infer how failure risk changes as a task progresses. Survival analysis models time-to-event data using hazard functions, and the log-logistic and Weibull distributions are common choices. A mixture model arises when observed data combine multiple underlying subpopulations, which can distort inferences if not accounted for.

Researchers introduced Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. The method maps token representations into concept activations, filters them with learned gates, pools them into layer-level summaries, and exposes them to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. It enables concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control while retaining useful predictive performance. GCA was evaluated on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. On toxicity detection, it remained close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline; on GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurred a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduced this gap; and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarified the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction.

The study finds that human references from the 2024 WMT MQM campaigns rank first in no campaign and contain annotated errors in 19% to 87% of segments, and that while learned metrics like xCOMET and MetricX are more robust than surface metrics, all metrics fail to detect named-entity contamination. This work challenges the foundational assumption of reference-based MT evaluation that human references are always correct and better than system outputs, which could impact how researchers and practitioners design and interpret evaluation metrics. The benchmark evaluates eight widely used metrics across three language pairs and finds that surface metrics show no length sensitivity, allowing contamination to hide in longer segments, while learned metrics accept references in unrelated languages as nearly correct. ReFocus introduces a progress-guided multi-round reinforcement learning framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. The framework alternates Global RL (full-task rollouts with DAG-based progress reward) and Local RL (additional interaction on Adaptive Practice Windows from an entry stage to a target stage), updating the entire policy throughout. TeamFlowRL is a two-stage framework that pretrains decentralized multi-agent flow policies offline and then fine-tunes them online by optimizing over full denoising trajectories with a shared team advantage, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, it improves every offline initialization with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score, and achieves 33.1% higher average success than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning on six bimanual tasks. By enabling effective online improvement of decentralized flow policies, TeamFlowRL could make generative policies practical for complex cooperative multi-agent tasks such as robot manipulation. The method formulates team policy optimization over complete denoising trajectories, weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage, and clips each ratio separately to align local updates with the team return. The empirical evaluation covers 51 paired configurations across seven simulation groups and six bimanual tasks, with all gains measured against offline initializations and Gaussian-policy fine-tuning baselines.

## [ReQOR: Training-Free Defense Against Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32755) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReQOR is a training-free defense that identifies and repairs dominant operator discrepancies caused by quantization on benign calibration data, mitigating Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) in LLMs. It formulates defense as repairing same-state operator discrepancies and restores full-precision computation along dominant directions in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. QCBs are an under-explored security threat where models behave maliciously only after quantization, and existing defenses often fail to pinpoint which changes to repair. ReQOR offers a principled, attack-agnostic solution that preserves benign utility and remains effective against non-PGD attacks where baselines fail. ReQOR isolates module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating high-precision and quantized modules on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory. It requires no attack information or gradient-based optimization, supports full-span and low-rank repair, and low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead while outperforming rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions.

**Background**: Quantization compresses large language models to lower precision for efficient deployment, but it can introduce vulnerabilities such as Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs), where a model behaves maliciously only after quantization while appearing benign at full precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but they do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. ReQOR addresses this by focusing on operator-level discrepancies between high-precision and quantized computations.
