## [Sleep-like recurrent passes improve in-context learning in transformer LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32802) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.32802) investigates whether a 'sleep' mechanism—performing N recurrent forward passes over a chunk of context—can improve in-context adaptation for transformer language models. The authors pre-train models up to 1.2B parameters on up to 100B tokens and find that longer sleep (larger N) enables faster few-shot learning on algorithmic and QA tasks, with N=2 and N=4 matching the no-sleep baseline's held-out code loss using 2.10x and 2.39x fewer in-context tokens, respectively. This work extends the sleep mechanism from SSM-attention hybrids to standard transformers and demonstrates concrete sample-efficiency gains on general, non-synthetic tasks, suggesting a path toward models that adapt from fewer examples. It also highlights a tradeoff between in-context adaptation and decoding latency, which is relevant for deploying sample-efficient LLMs in real-world applications. The study uses transformer language models up to 1.2B parameters trained on up to 100B tokens, and shows that longer sleep (larger N) not only speeds up in-context learning but also lowers next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. The abstract notes that the approach was previously validated only on within SSM-attention hybrid models for long-context reasoning, and the paper frames the work as a step toward better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: In-context learning refers to a language model's ability to perform a task by interpreting examples provided in the prompt without any weight updates. The 'sleep' mechanism, inspired by biological sleep, involves the model performing multiple recurrent forward passes over a context to iteratively refine its internal representations before the context is evicted from the attention cache. Prior work proposed this idea for SSM-attention hybrid architectures to improve long-context reasoning, but its effect on general in-context adaptation in pure transformers was unclear.

## [Residual Guidance Enables Prompt Switching in Streaming Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32820) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Residual Guidance (RG), a training-free method that counteracts context inertia in streaming video generation, allowing users to switch prompts mid-generation without losing visual continuity. RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk. This addresses a key limitation in real-time interactive video generation, where existing streaming models often ignore new prompts after a switch, hindering user control. RG improves prompt switching capability across various settings while retaining visual quality, and can be easily integrated into existing pipelines without training or per-model tuning. RG adds only one forward pass per chunk and requires no training or per-model tuning, making it computationally lightweight. It works by measuring a correction outside the cache, which avoids the visual continuity break that occurs when editing the cache directly.

**Background**: Streaming video generation models generate video chunk by chunk, using a cache of previous chunks to maintain temporal coherence. ## [PathGrad: Stable Gradients for Optimizing ML Force Fields Against Dynamical Observables](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32851) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PathGrad introduces a gradient estimator that differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of chaotic molecular trajectories, yielding stable gradients that accumulate on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives. The method was validated against finite-difference calculations and used to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients and structural constraints. This work solves the long-standing problem of unstable gradients when optimizing machine learning force fields against dynamical observables like diffusion coefficients, enabling direct refinement against experimental data. It could significantly improve the accuracy of ML potentials for computational chemistry and materials science, as demonstrated by better predictions of shear viscosity, rotational relaxation, and activation energies. The gradient estimator's variance remains stable as trajectory length increases, and alignment at a single temperature improves apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables. Notably, the optimized water potential also exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating improved fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) are data-driven models that approximate interatomic forces and potential energy, trained on quantum mechanical calculations. However, they inherit errors from the electronic-structure methods used to generate training data, and refining them against experimental measurements is challenging for dynamical properties because molecular trajectories are chaotic, leading to unstable gradients. Langevin dynamics adds friction and random noise to simulate thermal motion, and its path probabilities can be differentiated more stably than individual trajectories.

The study evaluates six LLMs across three formats, finding that MXFP4 benefits substantially from Hadamard rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation due to its finer-grained scales. Pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most accuracy lost at 4-bit and matches or exceeds a BF16 baseline on Llama-3.1-8B, while adding a per-tensor macroscale to MXFP4 does not improve average accuracy.

Researchers introduced Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget, solved via an iterative water-filling algorithm with provable convergence. Evaluations show up to 7.2 percentage points accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute, and on multi-turn video understanding, up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7–17.3x fewer TFLOPs. The plug-and-play nature means it can be integrated into existing video RAG pipelines without retraining, potentially benefiting applications like video question answering and surveillance analysis. Lembas captures two effects: the diminishing value of a token within each item and the decreased value as similar evidence receives more tokens, all in a single objective. For multi-turn conversations, it reuses tokens from earlier turns and refines relevance using the VLM's attention at no extra cost, with the water-filling algorithm guaranteeing convergence.

The study finds that VLMs largely cannot anticipate their weaknesses, but that information about these weaknesses emerges once the model begins solving the task. This work highlights a critical gap in model self-awareness, which matters for building reliable AI systems that can communicate their limitations and for developing methods to teach models about their own weaknesses. The study separates what a model knows about shared difficulty (tasks hard for all models) from what it knows about itself, and finds that VLMs misjudge overall accuracy and degraded-image effects. ## [ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection Using Frozen Speech Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33059) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ClusterVAD introduces a threshold-free unsupervised voice activity detection method that leverages frozen speech foundation model representations, clusters them, and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech using sonority. At inference, it computes frame-level speech probabilities from cluster assignments and applies a two-state hidden Markov model fitted per recording to enable threshold-free detection. This approach eliminates the need for labeled data and hand-crafted features, potentially improving robustness in challenging acoustic conditions such as far-field, noisy, or atypical speech. It could benefit speech processing pipelines like transcription and diarization by providing a more adaptable VAD component. ClusterVAD is fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech and achieves the lowest detection error on pause-level references across benchmarks including meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, while being competitive on speaker turn-level references. The use of a per-recording HMM allows threshold-free detection by modeling temporal continuity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Voice activity detection (VAD) is a fundamental step in speech processing that identifies speech segments in an audio stream. Traditional supervised VAD requires labeled data and may not generalize to new domains, while unsupervised methods often rely on hand-crafted features that degrade in noise. Speech foundation models are large pre-trained models that learn rich representations from unlabeled speech, and sonority is an acoustic measure of the inherent loudness of speech sounds, with vowels being more sonorous than consonants. Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are statistical models that can capture temporal dependencies and have been used in VAD to smooth frame-level decisions.

## [EventDiffusion learns native event stream distribution from videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33096) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EventDiffusion is a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings, decomposing generation into Event Activity Diffusion (EAD), Event Spatial Allocation (ESA), and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD). The authors also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric, and report that EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods across all datasets while remaining robust across different cameras at any resolution. Event cameras are data-hungry but real event recordings are scarce, so a method that synthesizes realistic native event streams from ordinary video could substantially expand training data for neuromorphic vision and event-based perception research. It also offers a principled alternative to hand-designed simulators whose prescribed sensor dynamics limit the diversity and fidelity of generated events. The framework explicitly models stochastic discrete event counts, distributes them to pixels while preserving cardinality, and learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions, rather than relying on estimated brightness trajectories. The CEFS metric combines event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity, and the method is claimed to generalize across cameras and resolutions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Event cameras are bio-inspired sensors that asynchronously record per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond temporal resolution and high dynamic range, producing sparse event streams rather than frames. Diffusion models are a class of generative models that learn to reverse a noising process, and they have become a powerful approach for image, video, and other data synthesis. Because event streams are asynchronous and sparse, generating realistic ones is harder than generating images, and existing simulators typically assume fixed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories.

A new arXiv paper (2611.33111) proposes post-hoc calibration of the draft model's output distribution in speculative decoding to reduce the distribution gap between draft and target models. The authors find that open-source draft models are generally underconfident compared to the target model, and show that standard temperature scaling improves acceptance length by up to approximately 10% with almost no additional cost. Speculative decoding is a key technique for accelerating LLM inference, but its speedup is limited by the acceptance rate of draft tokens. This work offers a simple, nearly free post-hoc fix that can be applied to existing draft models, potentially improving serving efficiency for practitioners without retraining. The method uses standard temperature scaling on the draft distribution, which improves acceptance length by up to ~10% across tasks with negligible overhead; throughput analysis confirms the serving efficiency gain. The paper also explores token-wise and more general calibration methods, revealing further potential room for improvement.

When the draft model's distribution deviates from the target's, acceptance rates drop, limiting the benefit of speculative decoding.

## [MADRA: Multi-Agent Debate for Risk-Aware Embodied Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21460) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MADRA introduces a training-free multi-agent debate architecture that uses a meta-cognitive Critical Agent to evaluate peer debates via a structured argumentation framework based on the Toulmin Model, mitigating herd mentality in multi-agent systems. The authors also release SafeAware-VH, a benchmark of adversarial safe instructions designed to probe agents' sensitivity to physical risks, and report that MADRA rejects over 90% of unsafe tasks while maintaining high utility, breaking the Pareto frontier compared to Chain-of-Thought and single-agent reflection baselines. This work addresses the safety-utility trade-off in LLM-based embodied planning, where safety alignment often causes over-rejection of benign household instructions, and could enable safer deployment of LLM agents in physical environments like homes and factories. The training-free nature makes it easy to integrate into existing systems without additional fine-tuning. MADRA is a cognitive architecture mimicking System-2 deliberation, and its Critical Agent uses the Toulmin Model's six components (claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier, rebuttal, backing) to structure arguments. The SafeAware-VH benchmark features adversarial safe instructions that probe physical risk sensitivity, and experiments show MADRA breaks the Pareto frontier with over 90% rejection of unsafe tasks while maintaining high utility.

## [AI Interpretability's 'Dead Salmon' Problem and a Statistical-Causal Fix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18792) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv position paper (2512.18792v2) argues that AI interpretability methods such as feature attribution, probing, sparse auto-encoding, and even causal analyses can produce plausible explanations for randomly initialized neural networks, mirroring the famous 'dead salmon' fMRI artifact. The authors propose a pragmatic statistical-causal reframing in which explanations are treated as parameters of a statistical model inferred from computational traces, and interpretability methods become statistical estimators tested against explicit alternative computational hypotheses. This critique matters because it challenges the validity of widely used interpretability techniques and warns that the field may be susceptible to false discoveries, poor generalizability, and high variance. If adopted, the proposed reframing could change how interpretability research is conducted and evaluated, affecting AI safety, model auditing, and trust in machine learning systems. The paper emphasizes that the issue goes beyond measuring statistical variability due to finite input sampling: it calls for uncertainty quantification with respect to the postulated statistical model and highlights theoretical issues such as the identifiability of common interpretability queries. As a position paper, it does not present new empirical benchmarks but rather a methodological argument and research agenda.

**Background**: The 'dead salmon' study refers to a 2009 neuroscience experiment in which a dead salmon placed in an fMRI scanner was shown images of humans in social situations, and standard analyses reported brain regions predictive of social emotions—a cautionary tale about misapplied statistical inference. In AI interpretability, researchers use methods like feature attribution (assigning importance to input features), probing (testing whether representations encode concepts), and sparse autoencoders (decomposing neural activations into sparse, interpretable features) to explain model behavior. ## [Survey Unifies Fairness of Explanations in AI, Exposing Procedural Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09852) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv survey (2605.09852v2) provides the first unified theoretical and literature review of fairness of explanations in AI, identifying a blind spot called procedural bias where models satisfy output fairness criteria but have unfair reasoning processes. It proposes a conditional invariance framework, a seven-dimensional taxonomy, three generative mechanisms of explanation inequity, and a six-step evaluation workflow. This work bridges algorithmic fairness and explainable AI, showing that standard fairness metrics on outputs are insufficient for responsible AI. It could influence how high-stakes domains like criminal justice, healthcare, credit, and employment audit and certify models, pushing for fairness audits of explanations. The conditional invariance framework formalizes explanation fairness as P(E(X) ∈ · | X_rel = x_rel, A = a) = P(E(X) ∈ · | X_rel = x_rel, A = b), from which existing metrics emerge as partial operationalizations. ## [TASTE: Reverse-Engineered Agent Benchmarks Expose Saturation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28556) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose TASTE (Task Synthesis from Tool Sequence Evolution), an automatic method that reverses benchmark construction by first sampling valid tool sequences using an Adaptive Contrastive n-gram model, then clustering and instantiating them into complete tasks. Using TASTE, they build τ^c-Bench, an extension of τ²-Bench, on which models that nearly saturate τ²-Bench suffer severe performance drops (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash falls from 0.82–0.94 to 0.28–0.61). This work shows that high scores on existing agent benchmarks often reflect saturation rather than robust task-solving ability, and it offers a scalable way to generate harder, higher-coverage benchmarks as agent capabilities advance. It could reshape how the community evaluates LLM agents and expose gaps that current benchmarks miss. TASTE uses an Adaptive Contrastive n-gram model trained on LLM-judged validity signals to sample valid tool sequences, then selects representative sequences via clustering and refines them through iterative difficulty evolution. The generated tasks more than double the number of unique tool combinations agents must execute, and evaluation across 11 agent/user LLM pairs confirms the difficulty increase.

DiSCO introduces a zero-shot, strictly black-box defense that operates entirely at the prompt level by performing distribution-guided suffix expansion via beam search and contrastive scoring over safe and unsafe image pools generated by the target model itself. DiSCO requires no model retraining, fine-tuning, or access to model internals, and it iteratively applies adaptive feedback until safe content is produced while maintaining semantic fidelity and improving image coherence. The defense is evaluated on the I2P benchmark under multiple red-teaming attacks, though the abstract is truncated and full experimental details are not provided.

## [Sparse Masks Govern Gradient Flow in Sinkhorn Attention Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07954) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.07954v2) proves that the sparsity pattern and marginal budgets of Sinkhorn attention layers control backward gradient flow, with gradients contracting at a rate given by the Dobrushin coefficient of an induced row-stochastic Markov kernel. The authors establish a face-lattice dichotomy showing that a mask and marginals guarantee score-uniform one-step contraction if and only if every nonempty face of the transportation polytope retains pairwise two-hop column overlap. This work gives practitioners a principled criterion for designing sparse masks in optimal-transport attention, showing that edge count, graph diameter, and forward reachability are insufficient to prevent gradient trapping. It also provides error bounds for both unrolled backpropagation and implicit differentiation, which could improve training stability and efficiency for Sinkhorn-based layers. The analysis shows that reverse-mode gradients propagate as zero-sum vectors whose total-variation norm contracts according to the kernel's Dobrushin coefficient, and that large learned scores can push the contraction rate arbitrarily close to one if the two-hop overlap condition fails. The paper extends the criterion to multi-layer schedules, proves exact one-sweep mixing for coordinate-factorized and butterfly masks, and derives closed-form bounds for expanders, local bands, and global hub tokens, with numerical checks verifying the finite-difference adjoints and spectral formulas.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Sinkhorn layers are differentiable optimal transport modules that normalize attention weights over a fixed sparse mask by alternating row and column scaling, enforcing capacity constraints on keys. They are used in attention mechanisms and multimodal alignment, where sparse masks are typically evaluated by edge count, graph diameter, or forward reachability. Backpropagation through Sinkhorn iterations can be done by unrolling or by implicit differentiation, and the convergence of these gradients is critical for stable training. The Dobrushin coefficient is a classical measure of contraction for Markov kernels in the total variation norm.

## [CALM: Prompt-Local Counterfactual Correction Outperforms Global Unsafety Removal in Text-to-Image Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02300) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02300v2) analyzes the limits of the global-unsafety assumption in training-free text-to-image safeguards and proposes CALM (Counterfactual Adaptive Local Modulation), a training-free method that replaces uniform global unsafe-direction removal with prompt-local counterfactual correction. CALM routes each prompt to active unsafe categories using matched unsafe-benign anchors, minimally edits only violating token representations toward the safe side, and suppresses positively aligned unsafe residual components, significantly improving unsafe content suppression while preserving benign utility. This work identifies a fundamental coverage-selectivity trade-off in existing global-unsafety safeguards: compact unsafe subspaces fail to cover heterogeneous unsafe semantics, while broader aggregation distorts safety-adjacent benign prompts. By offering a more selective, training-free alternative, CALM could influence the design of future safeguards for generative models, benefiting researchers and practitioners working on AI safety in text-to-image systems. The paper provides a controlled geometric analysis showing that compact unsafe subspaces fail to cover diverse unsafe semantics, whereas broader aggregation increasingly distorts safety-adjacent benign prompts. CALM is training-free and operates by minimally editing only violating token representations toward the safe side, using matched unsafe-benign anchors to route prompts to active unsafe categories.

## [ReTRACE: LLM Agent in Chemistry Harness for Retrosynthesis Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24744) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReTRACE is an LLM agent embedded in a deterministic chemistry harness that orchestrates molecular tools, single-step prediction engines, building-block libraries, and a multi-criterion evaluator for retrosynthesis planning. It introduces Audit@k, a two-stage metric combining programmatic structural checks with adversarial LLM review, and a three-stage post-training pipeline that distills trajectories into an open-weight coordinator, ReTRACE-27B, which raises Audit@1 from 11/40 (27.5%) to 23/40 (57.5%) on 40 evaluation targets. This work shows how LLM agents can be tightly coupled with deterministic chemistry tools to improve route-level judgment in retrosynthesis, a core problem in AI for science. The new Audit@k metric and the open-weight ReTRACE-27B model could provide a more reliable evaluation standard and a reusable coordinator for computational chemistry workflows. ReTRACE learns from harness feedback on two timescales: within a run it diagnoses weak sub-scores and backtracks to revise disconnections, and across runs it distills trajectories and audit verdicts into ReTRACE-27B. With GPT-6.2 Astra, it achieves Audit@1 of 97.9%, 99.3%, and 96.7% on Retro*-190, JMC2025, and FDA30, respectively, and two prospective wet-lab syntheses demonstrate that proposals translate into executable procedures after expert revision.

## [RegimeCouncil: Router for Memory Conflict Governance in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22113) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RegimeCouncil introduces a lightweight router that arbitrates between local and global memory suppression policies in LLM agents under hidden validity and delayed feedback, without retraining the LLM. It uses a Local Advisor, a Global Advisor, and an asymmetric Meta Governor that defaults to local scope and switches to global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. This work formulates memory conflict governance as an online choice problem and shows that neither fixed scope suffices alone, addressing a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems where stale memories can mislead actions. The approach outperforms the better fixed scope across 30 held-out settings, potentially improving reliability of agents in evolving environments. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor via off-path paired comparison or inverse-propensity estimation, and the method is evaluated on LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, with delays τ ∈ [1, 96], sparse or bandit feedback, using Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o. It achieves 5.2-7.3 points improvement on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, with microsecond overhead.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: LLM agents often store memories to inform future actions, but stored facts can become outdated as the world changes, creating conflicts between memory and reality. Existing systems typically hard-code either a local policy (suppress only the conflicting fact) or a global policy (suppress broadly), but neither is optimal under delayed feedback where the agent only later learns whether a memory was harmful. ## [Study finds rationale hallucination widespread in multimodal safety guards, proposes TCG-RL grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25793) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper systematically investigates rationale hallucination in multimodal safety guards, identifying two types: visual rationale hallucination (unsupported visual facts) and safety attribution hallucination (incorrect safety interpretation of grounded content). The authors show hallucination persists across rationale-generation methods, vision-language backbones, and datasets, and does not consistently diminish with higher accuracy or model scale, then propose Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning (TCG-RL) to reduce it. The findings reveal a gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, suggesting that current outcome-only evaluation of safety guards is insufficient. This matters for anyone deploying multimodal safety classifiers, as unreliable rationales could mislead human reviewers and downstream systems even when safety labels are correct. Analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows hallucination concentrates in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. TCG-RL rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference, substantially reducing hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance.

## [MixFold enables sub-4-bit mixed-precision LLM inference on mobile NPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26976) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MixFold introduces a method for executing 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations on mobile NPUs, avoiding weight expansion during decoding. It assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer mixed-precision assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. This work addresses a key bottleneck in deploying larger LLMs on mobile devices: sub-4-bit quantization often fails to speed up decoding on NPUs due to limited native datatype support. By achieving 1.16–1.41× faster decoding and 1.5–4.3× more tokens per joule than llama-cpp's Hexagon backend, MixFold could make sub-4-bit models practical for on-device inference. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights without converting them to wider datatypes on the vector unit, which would negate memory savings. Evaluated on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 across the Qwen3 model family, it achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama-cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Sub-4-bit quantization reduces model size by storing weights in 3 or 2 bits, but mobile NPUs like Qualcomm Hexagon have matrix units that support only a few native integer datatypes, so unsupported formats must be converted, often erasing speed gains. Mixed precision assigns different bit-widths to different parts of the model, but each matrix-unit tile can use only one datatype, limiting granularity. MixFold overcomes this by grouping output channels to align with tile boundaries, enabling fine-grained mixed precision without extra conversion overhead.

## [Randomized Forward Mode Offers Memory-Efficient Alternative to Backpropagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.14168) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces randomized forward mode gradient (RFG), a gradient estimator built from directional derivatives along random vectors, as an alternative to backpropagation. It establishes convergence guarantees for RFG-based gradient descent and Polyak's heavy ball methods on quadratic functions, showing that distributions with minimal kurtosis yield the fastest convergence. RFG can reduce memory usage by one to three orders of magnitude for parameter identification in differential equations, where computational graphs are long and parameter dimensions are small. This makes optimization feasible on memory-limited hardware, though it is not competitive for large-scale neural network training like physics-informed neural networks. The efficiency of RFG depends on the ratio of graph length to parameter dimension (ℓ/d): it is preferable when ℓ/d is large. However, RFG incurs a larger iteration count, making time to solution comparable to or worse than a well-tuned reverse mode with checkpointing.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Automatic differentiation (AD) computes derivatives of functions implemented as computer programs. Reverse mode AD (backpropagation) computes gradients in one sweep but stores intermediate results, leading to memory costs that grow with the computational graph length. Forward mode AD computes directional derivatives without storing a tape, but requires multiple passes for full gradients. RFG uses random directional derivatives to estimate the gradient, trading variance for memory efficiency.

## [Causal pieces measure expressivity of spiking neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14015) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces 'causal pieces', a novel concept that partitions the input and parameter space of feedforward spiking neural networks (SNNs) with single-spike coding into regions where the same subnetwork determines output spikes. For current-based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with large membrane time constants, the authors prove that within each causal piece, output spike times are locally Lipschitz continuous, and they derive a lower bound on approximation error that depends on the number of causal pieces. This work provides a principled theoretical tool for analyzing the expressivity and trainability of SNNs, which have been difficult to study due to spike-time discontinuities. The number of causal pieces serves as a measure of approximation capabilities, and experiments show that parameter initializations yielding more causal pieces correlate with training success, potentially impacting how SNNs are initialized and trained in practice. The theoretical results hold for networks of current-based LIF neurons with large membrane time constants, but simulations with standard single-spike LIF neurons indicate the findings extend beyond this regime. The analysis applies to networks with both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, and empirical validation on Yin-Yang, Fashion-MNIST, and EuroSAT benchmarks shows a strong correlation between the number of causal pieces on the training set and training success.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are artificial neural networks that mimic biological neurons by transmitting information through discrete spikes, with the timing of spikes carrying information. The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model is a prominent spiking neuron model where the neuron integrates incoming signals and fires when its membrane potential reaches a threshold. Lipschitz continuity is a mathematical property ensuring a function's rate of change is bounded, which is useful for analyzing stability and trainability. This paper adapts the concept of 'linear pieces' from artificial neural networks to SNNs, creating 'causal pieces' to study expressivity despite the discontinuous nature of spike times.

## [VFRTok: Variable Frame Rate Video Tokenizer with Duration-Proportional Information Assumption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12053) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VFRTok introduces a Transformer-based video tokenizer that uses asymmetric frame rate training between encoder and decoder to enable variable frame rate encoding and decoding, along with Partial Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to decouple position and content modeling. It achieves competitive reconstruction quality and state-of-the-art generation fidelity while using only 1/8 tokens compared to existing tokenizers. This work challenges the prevailing Frame-Proportional Information Assumption in video tokenization, potentially reducing the computational cost of diffusion-based video generation that currently scales linearly with frame rate. If adopted, it could make high-frame-rate video generation more efficient and accessible. The method is based on the Duration-Proportional Information Assumption, which posits that a video's information capacity upper bound is proportional to its duration rather than the number of frames. Partial RoPE groups correlated patches into unified tokens to improve content-awareness, and the code and weights are released on GitHub.

Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) encode positional information by rotating query and key vectors in attention, and are widely used in transformers for their ability to model relative positions. TRIM introduces a forward-statistics-based pruning wrapper that allocates different sparsity ratios to individual output rows while keeping model weights frozen, separating the scoring of which weights to prune from the allocation of how many to prune per row. The method composes with existing scorers and layer-wise allocations, making it broadly applicable to current pruning pipelines. TRIM is a forward-statistics-based wrapper that keeps weights frozen and separates scoring from allocation, allowing it to compose with existing scorers such as OWL and layer-wise allocation schemes. ## [CR-PPO: Complexity-Regularized PPO Replaces Entropy for Robust Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20509) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Complexity-Regularized Proximal Policy Optimization (CR-PPO), which replaces the standard entropy term in PPO with a self-regulating complexity term defined as the product of Shannon entropy and disequilibrium. This complexity measure is zero for both deterministic and uniform policies, maintaining beneficial stochasticity while reducing regularization pressure when the policy is highly uncertain. CR-PPO is significantly more robust to hyperparameter selection than entropy-regularized PPO, achieving consistent performance across orders of magnitude of regularization coefficients and remaining harmless when regularization is unnecessary. This reduces the need for expensive hyperparameter tuning, making PPO easier to deploy in practice. The complexity term is strictly positive only for policies exhibiting a meaningful interplay between order and randomness, and it automatically reduces regularization when the policy is highly uncertain. Empirical results show CR-PPO remains effective across a wide range of regularization coefficients, unlike entropy-regularized PPO which is sensitive to tuning.

However, maximizing entropy indiscriminately pushes the policy toward a uniform distribution, which can override the reward signal if not tuned properly. The proposed complexity measure, based on the product of Shannon entropy and disequilibrium, is zero for both fully deterministic and perfectly uniform distributions, thus favoring policies with a balance of order and randomness.

## [SparVAR: Training-Free Sparse Attention Accelerates Visual Autoregressive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04361) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SparVAR introduces a training-free acceleration framework for Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) modeling that exploits three observed attention properties—strong attention sinks, cross-scale activation similarity, and pronounced locality—to dynamically predict sparse attention patterns for high-resolution scales. It achieves a 1.57× speed-up over FlashAttention while preserving high-frequency details, and up to 2.28× when combined with scale-skipping strategies, reducing generation time of an 8B model producing 1024×1024 images to about 1 second. VAR models suffer from quartic attention complexity as resolution grows, causing substantial latency; SparVAR addresses this bottleneck without retraining or sacrificing image quality, making high-resolution generative modeling more practical. This could benefit researchers and practitioners deploying large VAR models for image generation, and the training-free nature allows easy integration with existing acceleration techniques. The method predicts sparse attention patterns from a sparse decision scale and constructs scale self-similar sparse attention via an efficient index-mapping mechanism, enabling block-wise sparse kernels that are over 5× faster than FlashAttention. It does not skip the final high-resolution scales, thus preserving high-frequency details, and code is available on GitHub.

## [CADTestBench: First Test-Based Benchmark for Text-to-CAD Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07807) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces CADTestBench, the first test-based benchmark for Text-to-CAD evaluation, built on CADTests—executable software tests that verify whether a generated CAD model meets the geometric and topological requirements of the input prompt. The authors benchmark recent Text-to-CAD methods and show that CADTests can also guide generation, yielding simple baselines that surpass current methods. Text-to-CAD evaluation has been a critical gap, and this test-based approach provides an objective, automated way to assess model performance, potentially accelerating design workflows and setting a new standard for the field. CADTestBench consists of 200 CAD programs derived from CADPrompt, each paired with an abstract and a detailed prompt, and is available on Hugging Face and GitHub. The tests check geometric and topological properties, and the benchmark code and data are publicly released.

## [External Detectors Beat Internal Warnings for Imposters in AI Agent Collectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09027) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.09027v4) shows that embedding imposter detection inside AI agent collectives is counterproductive, while a lightweight meta-trained external detector can rapidly adapt to unseen attacks from only a handful of examples. The study uses a deliberately small but challenging chess-based testbed and releases a benchmark of labeled deliberations spanning evolved imposter strategies. This work challenges the intuitive design of warning agents about possible imposters, showing it degrades decisions even without adversaries and leaks information. It offers a practical external detection approach for securing multi-agent systems, which is increasingly important as agentic AI deployments grow. The paper finds that simply warning agents of possible imposters is counterproductive: it degrades decisions even without adversaries, triggers unhelpful social dynamics, and leaks information to the imposter. The meta-trained external detector recalibrates to unseen attacks far more efficiently than conventional fine-tuning, and the benchmark includes labeled deliberations across a wide range of evolved imposter strategies.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Multi-agent systems, where multiple AI agents collaborate on complex tasks, can outperform single agents but are vulnerable to imposters that deliberately mislead peers. Detecting such imposters is challenging because even one can sabotage the collective. Meta-learning trains models across related tasks so they can adapt quickly to new tasks with little data, which is the technique used here for the external detector.

## [DISCA: Training-Free Cultural Alignment of LLMs via Persona Panels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10843) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DISCA is a training-free method that aligns frozen LLM moral preferences to specific countries by constructing persona panels from World Values Survey microdata and using consensus-based anchoring with loss-averse refinement. On the 20-country MultiTP benchmark, it reduces misalignment to human preference vectors by 10–24% on six of seven frozen backbones, and a 14B model with DISCA outperforms a vanilla 70B model. This work addresses the real problem of value misalignment across countries without requiring per-culture training data, per-country reward models, or access to model internals, making cultural alignment more accessible to underrepresented countries. It could enable more locally appropriate LLM deployments and inform AI ethics discussions on global fairness. DISCA keeps model weights frozen, reads only the model's score for each answer option, and uses a panel of four persona prompts per country; a loss-averse refinement is kept only when two independent runs agree, and a country-level prior pools decisions. It also improves social-norm classification on NormAd and moves answers closer to GlobalOpinionQA survey distributions than vanilla decoding.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Large language models often encode moral preferences that align most closely with one population, so a single deployment may impose one country's values on all users. Cultural alignment aims to adjust model outputs to better reflect local values, but existing methods typically require per-culture training data, reward models, or model internals. The World Values Survey is a global research program that collects microdata on changing values and beliefs across nearly 100 nations, providing a grounded source for country-specific preferences. Persona prompting is a technique that embeds explicit demographic or psychological attributes into LLM inputs to steer generation toward specific profiles.

## [Flash PD-SSM: Memory-Optimized Structured Sparse State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19150) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PD-SSM introduces a memory-optimized structured sparse state-space model that achieves finite-state automaton expressiveness comparable to unstructured matrices while maintaining the efficiency of structured SSMs. It maintains a trainable set of structured sparse matrices, one of which is discretely selected at each time-step, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on multivariate time-series tasks with sequences over 17,000 steps. This work addresses the fundamental trade-off between efficiency and expressivity in SSMs, potentially enabling more powerful sequence models without sacrificing scalability. It could impact hybrid LLMs and long-sequence modeling by providing a drop-in replacement that improves state-tracking and language modeling with less memory than DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. PD-SSM matches the training speed of widely used SSMs up to 3B parameters while using less memory than DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. The code is available at https://github.com/IBM/flash-pdssm, and the model's theoretical expressivity is validated on synthetic mechanistic and state-tracking tasks.

**Background**: State-space models (SSMs) are a class of sequence models that process inputs through a hidden state governed by a transition matrix. The structure of this matrix determines a trade-off: unstructured matrices are highly expressive but computationally expensive, while structured matrices are efficient but limited in expressivity, particularly in emulating finite-state automata (FSA). Recent work on structured sparse SSMs, such as PD-SSM, aims to bridge this gap by using sparse transition matrices that retain efficiency while improving expressivity.

## [NPSolver: Label-Free Neural Poisson Solver with Iterative Physics Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25786) ⭐️ 7.0/10

NPSolver is a neural Poisson solver trained without solution labels by using a few preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) steps to refine its own predictions, providing a stable and well-scaled training signal. It also introduces the Boundary-Aware Transolver (BA-Transolver) architecture that separates interior and boundary tokenization to better handle mixed boundary conditions. This approach eliminates the need for large-scale labeled datasets and avoids the unstable training dynamics of physics-informed residual losses, making neural PDE solvers more practical for complex, irregular domains. It could benefit scientific machine learning and numerical methods communities by enabling fast, reliable solutions and gradient-based boundary control. Theoretical analysis confirms that the iterative supervision acts as a well-conditioned error proxy and that a stop-gradient design is essential for optimization stability. Evaluations on 2D and 3D irregular geometries show NPSolver outperforms physics-informed and data-driven baselines, and a downstream thermal control task demonstrates efficient gradient-based boundary control.

**Background**: The Poisson equation is a fundamental partial differential equation in scientific computing, but classical iterative solvers can be prohibitively slow on complex, irregular domains due to ill-conditioned systems. Neural operators learn mappings between function spaces to provide fast approximate solutions, but they typically require large labeled datasets or suffer from unstable training when using physics-informed residual losses. Preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) is an iterative method for solving symmetric positive definite linear systems, often used to accelerate convergence in numerical PDE solvers.

## [Stakeholder Grounding Exercise Reveals Text Embeddings Misalign with Expert Associations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27168) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Stakeholder Grounding Exercise, a method to make expert associations explicit and measure alignment between text embeddings and human experts. In a Danish policy case study, embeddings show an 18-27 percentage point reliability gap compared to experts, and this misalignment propagates to downstream clustering (Spearman ρ = 0.86); a US AI use case study replicates the gap (16.1pp) in English. This work highlights that widely used text embeddings may not capture the semantic distinctions that domain experts care about, potentially leading to invalid analyses in applied settings. It offers a practical, lightweight method for researchers and practitioners to assess embedding models before using them in high-stakes clustering or analysis tasks. The gap is measured as a percentage point difference in reliability between embeddings and experts, and the strong Spearman correlation (ρ = 0.86) between exercise rankings and cluster quality indicates that misalignment directly affects clustering outcomes. The replication across two languages and domains (Danish policy and US AI use cases) suggests the gap is not an artifact of a single instrument or community.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Text embeddings are vector representations of text that capture semantic meaning, widely used for clustering, search, and classification. Representational alignment refers to whether these embeddings encode the same semantic relations as human experts, which is crucial for valid analyses. The Stakeholder Grounding Exercise is a protocol that elicits expert associations to ground embedding model selection in human judgment.

## [eXTC: Three-Stage Method for Interpretable Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29076) ⭐️ 7.0/10

eXTC introduces a three-stage approach that learns a natural language rulebook (SOP) via Structured Prompt Optimization, distills reasoning from a large teacher LLM into a compact model, and then expands capabilities with reinforcement learning. This enables fast inference with local reasoning traces and a global modular explanation of learned rules, outperforming existing paradigms on diverse benchmarks. This work addresses the trade-off between scalable but opaque supervised fine-tuning and interpretable but less performant discrete prompt optimization, offering a practical solution for interpretable and efficient text classification. It could impact applications requiring transparency, such as healthcare or finance, and advance research in explainable AI. The method uses a compact language model for fast inference, provides local reasoning traces at inference time, and a global modular explanation of domain rules. Stage-by-stage gains are reported, but the approach relies on a large teacher LLM for distillation and may require careful tuning of the RL stage.

## [FLIPS fingerprints individual LLM instances via pseudo-random sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03330) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced FLIPS, an instance-level fingerprinting method that distinguishes different configurations of the same LLM by exploiting biases in generated binary random sequences. On a benchmark of 237 model instances, FLIPS identified the target instance with 77% accuracy using only 32 queries, versus at most 33% for an adapted LLMmap baseline. Current fingerprinting techniques are designed for intellectual property protection and are deliberately robust to instance-level parameter changes, which is the opposite of what regulators need when assessing actual deployed behavior. FLIPS reframes fingerprinting as a regulator-oriented tool that can identify the specific configuration behind a deployed model, potentially supporting compliance assessments for safety and toxicity risks. The method works by analyzing biases in binary random sequences generated by the model, and the authors note that the open-set challenge—recognizing an unseen target—remains much harder: with 10% unseen instances, FLIPS achieved 41% recall at 23% precision, more than twice random. Closed-set instance fingerprinting is thus practical with a few dozen queries, while open-set identification remains an open problem.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: LLM fingerprinting is the practice of identifying a model from its response behavior rather than metadata, typically using carefully crafted queries; existing methods like LLMmap focus on identifying model families or versions for IP protection. However, an LLM's behavior also depends on instance-level parameters such as the instructional prompt, sampling configuration (e.g., temperature, top-p), and quantization, so the same model can behave very differently across deployments. FLIPS targets this gap by distinguishing configurations of the same underlying model rather than identifying its provenance.

LLM-ACES introduces a closed-loop framework that uses a large language model to propose operator priors constraining symbolic search while adaptively acquiring informative trajectories, improving recovery of governing ODEs from limited data. On 122 ODE systems from ODEBench and ODEBase, it achieves the lowest median NMSE and up to 70.8% and 69.5% symbolic accuracy, respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. This work addresses the identifiability gap in data-driven ODE discovery by jointly optimizing hypothesis construction and data acquisition, which could make equation discovery more reliable in scientific domains where observations are scarce or noisy. It represents a step toward more autonomous AI-for-science systems that actively design experiments rather than passively fitting fixed datasets. LLM-ACES is sample-efficient, achieving better performance with less data, and under observation noise and sparse sampling it maintains the lowest reconstruction error without inflating expression complexity, whereas baselines tend to add spurious terms. The code is available at https://github.com/scientific-discovery/LLM-ACES.

## [Pramana: A Composable Backend for Empirical Networking Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26352) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Pramana proposes a composable, domain-specific backend that generates experimental data on demand for empirical networking research, using a thin-waist architecture that separates research intents from execution substrates. The authors built a corpus of 255 data-generation intents from 66 published papers, showed that their intent specification expresses all of them while no existing tool covers more than 11%, and demonstrated a proof-of-concept implementation covering 27% of intents, including regenerating data for one trial of each network setting and congestion-control algorithm in the CCAnalyzer paper's main experiment. This work addresses the 'ideation-to-data gap' in empirical networking research, where AI agents can propose hypotheses faster than researchers can generate data to test them. The intent specification separates what data a study needs (intent) from where it is generated (substrate) and how it is produced (mechanism), allowing one specification to target any substrate. However, the current proof-of-concept only covers 27% of the 255 intents, and the authors note that implementing the full design requires a community effort.

## [Parameter-Free Dynamic Regret Achieved Under Heavy-Tailed Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27073) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper derives tight minimax dynamic regret bounds for online convex optimization with heavy-tailed subgradient noise (p-th moment, p in (1,2]) and presents a parameter-free algorithm that combines AdaGrad learners restarted at different frequencies via exponential weights. The algorithm attains the optimal rate without knowing the subgradient bound G, noise scale σ, moment order p, or path length P_T. This work closes a gap in online convex optimization by providing the first minimax optimal dynamic regret bounds under heavy-tailed noise, which is more realistic than bounded or sub-Gaussian assumptions. It enables robust online learning in non-stationary environments where gradient noise may have infinite variance, impacting algorithm design in learning theory and stochastic optimization. The minimax expected dynamic regret is shown to be, up to constants, min{GD√(TΛ_T) + σDT^{1/p}Λ_T^{(p-1)/p}, GDT}, where Λ_T = 1 + P_T/D. The algorithm's constant for the noise term is O(1+log(p/(p-1))) and no logarithmic factor of T appears; running on doubling epochs removes the need to know T at the cost of a factor 2+√2.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Online convex optimization (OCO) is a framework for sequential decision-making where a learner predicts with convex loss functions and aims to minimize regret—the difference between cumulative loss and that of the best comparator. Dynamic regret compares against a sequence of comparators that can change over time, with path length P_T measuring total movement. Heavy-tailed noise refers to stochastic gradients whose variance may be infinite, modeled by a finite p-th moment with p<2. Parameter-free algorithms adapt to unknown problem parameters without tuning.

## [UniDFKD: Architecture-Agnostic Data-Free Distillation via Explicit Semantics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09287) ⭐️ 7.0/10

UniDFKD proposes a unified data-free knowledge distillation framework that replaces architecture-specific statistical priors, such as Batch Normalization statistics, with explicit architecture-agnostic semantic conditioning. It governs synthesis and distillation through three components—Categorical Semantic Conditioning, Spatial Semantic Anchoring, and Spatial Semantic Distillation—and outperforms the strongest baseline NAYER by average absolute margins of 17.23 and 24.49 in top-1 accuracy under homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, respectively. This work addresses a real limitation in data-free knowledge distillation: existing methods rely on BatchNorm statistics that are absent in modern architectures like Vision Transformers, causing severe performance degradation. By making DFKD architecture-agnostic, it enables model compression for ViTs and other modern models without access to original training data, which is valuable for privacy-sensitive and resource-constrained deployments. The framework's three components respectively define what to synthesize via language-derived embeddings, regularize where evidence belongs by anchoring teacher spatial attributions to a Gaussian prior, and control knowledge transfer by aligning teacher-student spatial evidence alongside predictions. Experiments cover both CNNs and ViTs, though the paper is a specialized arXiv preprint without community discussion or peer review yet.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation compresses a large pretrained teacher model into a smaller student model by transferring its learned behavior. GEM treats encoding as conceptually processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation, and it learns embeddings aligned with its own reasoning rather than performing conventional query expansion. ## [LEDGER Algorithm Achieves Near-Optimal Regret for Noisy Online Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06921) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LEDGER, an algorithm for online convex optimization with time-varying constraints observed only through bounded-variance noise. It achieves O(√T) expected regret and O(√(T log T)) expected budget violation over T rounds, using one projection per round and requiring no strictly feasible action. This work provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for online learning under noisy constraint observations, a setting common in real-world applications where constraints are estimated rather than known exactly. It also establishes matching lower bounds, showing the logarithmic factor is necessary and delineating the limits of what is achievable. The algorithm uses a signed budget violation measure (maximum total overspend over any interval) and achieves O(√T) regret with O(√(T log T)) violation; a lower bound shows that O(√T) violation forces linear regret, and for hard violation (sum of positive parts), no algorithm can keep both regret and violation sublinear under unknown noise distributions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Online convex optimization (OCO) is a framework where a learner sequentially chooses actions and incurs convex losses, with performance measured by regret against the best fixed action in hindsight. Time-varying constraints require the learner to satisfy different constraints each round, and prior work typically assumes exact constraint observations. This paper relaxes that assumption to noisy observations, which is more realistic but complicates the analysis.

By preserving full spatial coverage while compacting semantics, Varest could enable cheaper and faster multimodal inference without sacrificing accuracy, and its generalization to modern VLMs like Qwen3.8-27B suggests broad applicability. Varest uses object boundaries distilled from a visual foundation model to guide token grouping and text localization to protect details needed for reading, with a granularity dial that merges into coarser regions at lower budgets. A learned selector then prunes visual tokens after early language decoder layers, reducing repeated access to already integrated information.

## [RAINFALL: LLM-Driven Ranking Function Synthesis for Loop Termination Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35523) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RAINFALL is a neuro-symbolic framework that formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the program that the LLM fills in four predefined slots per loop. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, it synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 of 358 terminating C programs (93.02%), outperforming PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category, by 22 programs. Ranking function synthesis is a core but notoriously difficult problem in program termination analysis, and this work shows that LLMs combined with symbolic verification can surpass a state-of-the-art dedicated termination tool. The generate-verify-refine paradigm offers a reusable template for other formal-methods tasks where correctness must be guaranteed. The framework uses a generate-verify-refine loop: a symbolic verifier checks the LLM's output, and verification failures are translated into natural-language diagnostics that guide iterative refinement. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback, and combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 raises the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: A ranking function is a mathematical expression that decreases with every loop iteration and is bounded below, which proves that the loop must eventually terminate. Synthesizing such functions automatically is hard because it requires finding the right expression form and proving it decreases, often needing substantial human expertise. Neuro-symbolic approaches pair neural models like LLMs, which can propose candidate solutions, with symbolic verifiers that provide formal guarantees. The generate-verify-refine paradigm iteratively improves LLM outputs by feeding verification failures back as feedback.

## [ResCom: Low-Rank Activation Residual Compensation Boosts LLM Quantization Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ResCom introduces a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for layer-output errors in low-bit weight-activation quantized LLMs, computed in closed form without gradient training or weight updates. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96% to 36.16%. This method significantly improves the accuracy of low-bit quantized LLMs without retraining, making deployment more practical and cost-effective. The strong empirical gains, especially on reasoning tasks like GSM8K, could accelerate adoption of 4-bit weight-activation quantization in production inference. The FP32 implementation adds 2.25% to 4K prefill time, while a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7% peak-memory reduction relative to FP16. Evaluations span models from 1B to 70B parameters and include held-out C4 tests, demonstrating generality beyond the Llama-3-8B setting.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Low-bit weight-activation quantization reduces memory and computation for deploying large language models, but activation rounding can degrade accuracy after calibration because reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. Low-rank correction techniques add a low-rank residual to a quantized weight matrix or attach a low-rank path to a compressed layer to compensate for quantization error. ResCom specifically targets activation rounding residuals, using an output-aware calibration procedure to select residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction.

## [Margin Graph Fixes Feature Selection Flaw in SAE Attribution Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00606) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a 'margin graph' that re-selects features after predicting score changes, addressing a limitation in sparse autoencoder attribution graphs that ignore features entering or leaving the TopK selection. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. This work identifies a fundamental flaw in attribution graphs used for mechanistic interpretability and offers a simple fix that significantly improves prediction of which features change. It could lead to more accurate interpretability tools for understanding language model internals, benefiting AI safety and transparency research. The margin graph adds the predicted change to every score and re-selects, but when written back into the model, its coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject-verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. This indicates that better predicting feature selection changes does not necessarily translate to better predicting model output on the tested task and SAE pair.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used in mechanistic interpretability to decompose a language model's activations into sparse, interpretable features. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest, and a feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. Attribution graphs predict how interventions affect downstream features using derivatives taken before the intervention, but they keep the original selection and thus miss features that enter or leave the TopK set.

Trained on 5s clips, it achieves the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60s and 240s, outperforming SGF by 3.6 and 6.1 points in aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.

## [Visual Backdoors Persist in On-Policy Distillation for VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22446) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.22446v3) challenges the assumption that On-Policy Distillation (OPD) inherently resists backdoor propagation in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, combined with theoretical analysis, the authors show that visual backdoors can still propagate via OPD, with attack success rate rapidly approaching 100% once a critical poisoning ratio is exceeded. This research reveals an overlooked security risk in a popular post-training paradigm for VLMs, suggesting that even distillation methods thought to be safe can transfer malicious behaviors from teacher to student. It has implications for AI safety and ML security, especially as OPD becomes more widely adopted for training multimodal models. Unlike traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios, but attack success rate jumps to nearly 100% past a threshold; propagation is driven by accumulation of anomalous probability mass from the teacher rather than explicit malicious responses. The authors also propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is a post-training method where a student model generates its own response trajectories and is supervised by the teacher's probability distributions, rather than by fixed teacher-generated responses. It has emerged as an efficient alternative to reinforcement learning for aligning large models. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process both images and text, and backdoor attacks aim to implant hidden triggers that cause malicious behavior when activated. Prior work has shown that conventional knowledge distillation can propagate backdoors from teacher to student, but OPD's resistance was previously assumed.

## [Hypnos: Dual-Phase Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24637) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Hypnos is an open-source dual-phase platform for continual learning at the edge, using a wake phase with lightweight gradient-free prototype updates on a RISC-V MCU and a sleep phase with rehearsal-based gradient updates on a smart charger. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% on CORe50 NICv2-391, with 3.8x fewer learning steps and 22x less learning compute than quantized latent replay. This work addresses the key challenge of online continual learning on resource-constrained edge devices, enabling private and adaptive AI without cloud dependency. The dual-phase design inspired by wake/sleep cycles could make continual learning practical for low-power IoT and embedded systems. The platform is deployed on a ZCU104 FPGA and synthesized in 28nm, with on-device latency of 7.79-10.54 seconds per sample depending on activation precision. The wake phase uses gradient-free prototype updates, while the sleep phase leverages wall-plug energy and larger memory for rehearsal-based consolidation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Continual learning aims to let neural networks adapt to new data over time without catastrophically forgetting previous knowledge. Edge devices like microcontrollers have tight power and memory budgets, making traditional backpropagation training impractical. Hypnos draws inspiration from the brain's wake-sleep cycle: rapid adaptation during the day and memory consolidation during sleep.

## [VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27381) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VMSA proposes a video memory skill agent that combines three complementary structured memory components—segment captions, entity events, and entity-aware episodes—to improve retrieval and reasoning for long-video question answering. It achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench. This work addresses the hard problem of retrieving and integrating evidence across hours-long videos, which is critical for applications like egocentric assistants and video surveillance. By jointly designing structured memories and memory skills, it advances agentic approaches for long-video understanding and could influence future multimodal LLM systems. VMSA constructs Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad context to guide retrieval and reasoning. It also induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification.

## [Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth and Ego-Motion from Event Cameras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27509) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.27509v2) proposes a self-supervised method that assigns each event its own depth in continuous time and recovers camera motion from the same asynchronous event stream, using geometric consistency and differentiable rendering. On the MVSEC benchmark, it outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. This work shows that motion-compensated event alignment can serve as a principled supervision signal for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation, avoiding the need for costly dense depth ground truth and preserving the microsecond timing that distinguishes event cameras. It could benefit robotics, autonomous navigation, and event-based vision where low-latency, high-dynamic-range perception is critical. The method lifts each event into 3D using its predicted depth and displaces it by the camera motion at the instant it fired, so misalignment between events from the same edge exposes errors in depth or motion; differentiable rendering then produces dense depth maps at target times within each window. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Event cameras are neuromorphic sensors that asynchronously report per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond precision, rather than capturing full frames at a fixed rate. This makes them attractive for high-speed, high-dynamic-range scenarios, but the resulting stream is sparse and irregular, and dense depth ground truth is expensive to acquire. Self-supervised depth estimation typically learns from photometric or geometric consistency instead of labeled depth, while differentiable rendering enables end-to-end optimization by providing gradients through the rendering process.

## [LLMs show more social sycophancy via consumer UIs than APIs, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28012) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv study tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both their consumer user interfaces (UIs) and application programming interfaces (APIs) across four dimensions of social sycophancy. It found that UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]), though differences varied significantly across models, including a reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). This finding suggests that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in consumer-facing systems, which has important implications for AI safety and evaluation methodology. It highlights that access conditions are consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluations and could affect how developers and researchers assess model behavior. The study released 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation. The large variation across models and dimensions, including the DeepSeek reversal, indicates that sycophancy is not uniformly affected by access mode and that model-specific factors play a significant role.

## [Grammar-as-a-Drafter boosts speculative decoding for structured outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28349) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Grammar-as-a-Drafter (GaaD) makes the grammar engine a second drafter in speculative decoding, merging grammar-forced tokens into the draft before each verification step. On a JSON benchmark, GaaD raised average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP and delivered 2.66–2.81x faster decoding at batch size 1. Structured outputs like JSON schemas and tool-call formats are increasingly common in production LLM applications, where speculative decoding often stalls because drafters propose tokens that violate the grammar. GaaD composes with any drafter without adding kernels or compilation on the critical path, potentially making constrained generation substantially faster for latency-sensitive serving. The scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens (out-degree 1 in the grammar automaton) into a draft row of width K, promoting matching tokens to GRAMMAR and truncating the proposal where it disagrees. Accepting canonical GRAMMAR drafts with probability 1 preserves grammar validity but can shift the output distribution relative to grammar-masked decoding, and GaaD modestly raises plain-text TPOT under mixed traffic.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM generation by having a lightweight drafter propose several tokens that the target model verifies in a single forward pass, accepting the longest matching prefix. Grammar-constrained decoding enforces formal rules, such as a context-free grammar or JSON schema, during generation to guarantee syntactically valid structured output. Under such constraints, the drafter is unaware of the grammar and frequently proposes invalid keys, delimiters, or indentation, wasting verification slots.

## [PixelOne: Single-Pass GUI Grounding at Native Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30235) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PixelOne introduces a single-forward-pass GUI grounding method that distills spatial knowledge from a search-based teacher to a student model, enabling precise click prediction directly from native-resolution screenshots. Its PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B variant achieves 83.8% mean accuracy across four benchmarks with 0.43 s mean latency per target, the highest among evaluated single-forward grounders. This work addresses a key trade-off in GUI automation: downsampling screenshots loses detail needed for small controls, while fixed global bins become inefficient at higher resolutions. By achieving high accuracy in a single forward pass at native resolution, PixelOne could make multimodal GUI agents faster and more reliable for real-world interaction tasks. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions, while the student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, a decision head selects a visual token and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, with a click-aligned loss encouraging pixels inside the target box to score above those outside.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: GUI grounding is the task of mapping a natural-language instruction to a specific clickable element on a screen, a core capability for multimodal agents that operate software interfaces. Prior approaches like GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement, but screenshot downsampling removes fine detail and fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. Knowledge distillation is a technique where a smaller student model learns to mimic a larger or more complex teacher model, and spatial distillation specifically transfers spatial knowledge such as feature maps or attention distributions. VideoJEV is a system-one model that replaces autoregressive text generation with a scorer that rates candidate options against cached video evidence, enabling fast single-pass inference.
