A new framework generates molecules de novo that are predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles by constructing a panoramic binding matrix over 20 olfactory receptors, clustering it to find representative patterns, and using reinforcement learning with a structured selectivity loss. Across nine target profiles, the method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18,000 oracle calls, with the largest gains on rare profiles such as broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets. This work connects molecular generation with the combinatorial code of olfaction, potentially enabling the design of odorants with desired smells for the flavor, fragrance, and consumer product industries. It also demonstrates a general reinforcement learning approach for targeting multi-receptor activity profiles, which could inspire similar strategies in drug discovery where polypharmacology is important. The structured selectivity loss combines pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints to steer the generator, and the method is evaluated on nine target profiles of varying complexity. ## [iTDM Fixes Gradient Drift in Diffusion RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30986) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies that existing forward diffusion reinforcement learning methods rely on signed reward-weighted regression with an idealized behavior-policy assumption that breaks under classifier-free guidance and off-policy settings, causing baseline-induced gradient drift. It proposes Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), which takes the infinitesimal limit of trajectory distribution matching to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity, ensuring exact baseline invariance without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. This work addresses a fundamental theoretical flaw in diffusion RL, potentially improving training stability and sample efficiency for aligning diffusion models with human preferences. It could benefit researchers and practitioners working on text-to-image generation, compositional generation, and other diffusion-based applications where reinforcement learning from feedback is used. iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL, converging nearly 3× faster on GenEval2 and scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. It also scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, with code available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Diffusion models generate data by iteratively denoising random noise, and classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a widely used technique to improve sample quality by combining conditional and unconditional predictions. Reinforcement learning (RL) for diffusion models often uses reward-weighted regression (RWR), where the policy is trained to regress onto rollouts weighted by rewards. Forward diffusion RL enables deterministic ODE sampling without backpropagating through the entire trajectory, making alignment more efficient.

## [Frequency-Conditioned Privacy Auditing of Fine-Tuned Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31581) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper studies how the frequency of sensitive data (email addresses and phone numbers) in fine-tuning corpora affects their recoverability from four language models, comparing standard fine-tuning, gradient clipping, and differentially private training (DP-SGD). The authors vary repetition from 1x to 50x and find that the number of repetitions needed for extraction varies substantially across models, with DP-SGD at ε=5 showing zero observed extraction up to 50x repetition. This work provides practical guidance for organizations fine-tuning LLMs on sensitive data, showing that simple repetition thresholds for privacy risk are model-dependent and that gradient clipping alone is insufficient at high repetition. It reinforces differential privacy as a robust mitigation, though with utility trade-offs, informing data curation and training choices. The study tests four language models and finds that gradient clipping can delay extraction but does not consistently prevent leakage at high repetition, while DP-SGD at ε=5 yields zero observed extraction through 50x repetition across all models under the tested attacks, with utility cost varying by model. Code and data are publicly available.

## [Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31932) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CPSD introduces a contrastive on-policy self-distillation framework for LLM unlearning that constructs a knowledge-reduced target distribution along the model's own trajectories. A frozen reference model evaluates each token under a plain context and a privileged context containing the forget information, and the resulting distributional shift is reversed to obtain a counterfactual unlearning target that the student is trained to match at every rollout position. This work addresses a key limitation of likelihood-based unlearning methods, which optimize against fixed forget sequences and provide only negative supervision while ignoring the states visited by the evolving unlearned policy. Experiments under OpenUnlearning show CPSD improves the forgetting-utility trade-off over NPO across TOFU forget-set sizes and Llama models from 1B to 8B parameters, suggesting a more effective approach for removing designated training data while preserving unrelated capabilities. The framework also includes a privacy-enhanced variant that combines distributional unlearning with lightweight sequence-level suppression, and on MUSE-News this variant improves all reported knowledge, memorization, privacy, and utility metrics over NPO. The approach relies on a frozen reference model and privileged context containing forget information, and its impact is yet to be validated beyond the reported benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Large language model unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data so that the model behaves as if it never saw that information, while retaining its essential knowledge and unrelated capabilities. On-policy self-distillation is a technique in which a single model acts as both teacher and student with different contexts, using privileged information to guide its own generations. Contrastive learning, meanwhile, leverages distributional shifts between contexts to learn discriminative representations, and CPSD combines these ideas by treating the distributional shift caused by forget information as a knowledge-associated direction to be reversed.

Researchers present CAPE, a training-free compiler that interleaves calibration and search to compile tool-use policies under unknown tool configurations. On CSV and JSON workflows built from 64 requests, CAPE reaches the independently computed optimum in 502 of 504 compilations while taking 22.0% less compilation time than eager exact search. Tool calls can fail when the receiving tool parses delimiters, dates, or record layouts under an uninspectable configuration, so CAPE's ability to maintain an executable policy while directing calibration to useful calls could make LLM agents more robust in real-world tool integration. CAPE maintains an executable policy at all times, directs calibration to calls that can improve this policy, and tightens bounds only where doing so ends calibration early. Returned policies preserve every configuration the initial policy completes, and CAPE certifies optimality when its executable and optimistic values meet.

## [Marginal-only predictors underestimate total correlation in diffusion LM parallel decoding by about one bit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31990) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper estimates the conditional total correlation C lost when committing multiple tokens in parallel decoding of masked diffusion language models, and finds that the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17 bits) on three of four models. On a subset, the estimate ranks candidate sets similarly to the exact KL cost but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it, with Dream-instruct being an exception mainly on prose. This analysis quantifies how much dependency information is lost when decoders use per-position marginals to select tokens for parallel commits, which is relevant for designing faster and more accurate diffusion language model inference. It provides a measurement methodology and highlights that most of the predictive accuracy comes from a simple bound, suggesting room for dependency-aware decoding improvements. The measurement requires a validated readout because Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and using the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times; the authors provide three checks to measure the convention. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons, and the results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not the gains of a dependency-aware decoder.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Masked diffusion language models generate text by iteratively denoising a fully masked sequence in parallel, committing multiple tokens per step to speed up inference. Each token is sampled from its own marginal distribution, so dependencies between simultaneously committed tokens are ignored, and the lost dependency is measured by the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders select tokens using per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it exactly.

## [Monadic Alpha-Beta Pruning Using Continuation and Reader Monads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32320) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents a monadic formulation of alpha-beta pruning that combines the continuation monad and the reader monad, recording alpha-beta bounds within monadic outcomes rather than in the types of moves. The approach is demonstrated with a Tic-Tac-Toe implementation that achieves a 39-fold reduction in the number of plays evaluated compared to exhaustive search, and the authors formally prove correctness against exhaustive minimax search. This work shows how a foundational game AI algorithm can be expressed and verified using standard monadic abstractions, providing a basis for compositional approaches to adversarial search. It may be valuable to researchers in functional programming and game AI who are interested in principled, type-safe implementations of search algorithms. Unlike previous approaches that encode alpha-beta bounds into the types of available moves, this construction leaves move types unchanged and records bounds in monadic outcomes. The ordinary continuation monad suffices to compute both optimal outcomes and optimal plays by extending the outcome type to include move sequences, offering an alternative to generalizations of the continuation monad proposed to address inefficiencies of the selection monad in alpha-beta search.

The method uses a two-stage training process: after reasoning fine-tuning, it routes rollouts based on quality, with erroneous ones receiving privileged token-level supervision from successful siblings. During inference, disagreement among rollouts triggers pairwise refinement of uncertain assignments, but the approach requires multiple rollouts and may increase inference cost.

A new arXiv paper (2611.31320) disentangles three factors in EEG foundation models: how representations are read out, whether intermediate layers provide predictive utility beyond the final layer, and whether depth structure transfers across datasets. Across five models and three tasks, the authors find that improving the final-layer readout recovers substantial performance, yet intermediate layers remain advantageous under frozen extraction, and layers selected on one dataset remain useful on another across five dataset pairs and four task families. The findings suggest that predictive utility varies across depth and depends on readout and transfer, but the gains are incremental and the study is limited to the selected models and tasks.

The paper introduces progressive posterior sampling (PPS) with manifold projection, a method that automatically estimates measurement noise variance and avoids singular value decomposition (SVD) of the measurement operator. During reverse diffusion, PPS constructs a closed-form Gaussian approximation to the posterior and projects the guided sample onto a spherical level set to maintain consistency with the local image manifold. This work removes two common practical requirements in diffusion-based inverse problem solving—SVD computation and prior knowledge of noise variance—making the approach more broadly applicable. It could benefit researchers and practitioners in computational imaging, where such inverse problems are central. PPS is evaluated on FFHQ and ImageNet across four restoration tasks and three measurement noise levels, showing competitive reconstruction accuracy and perceptual quality. The method relies on a spherical level set approximation of the local noisy image manifold, which may introduce assumptions about manifold geometry.

**Background**: Diffusion models are generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process, and they can serve as powerful priors for solving inverse problems such as denoising, super-resolution, and deblurring. Posterior sampling in this context aims to draw samples from the conditional distribution of clean images given noisy measurements, often requiring approximations because the true posterior is intractable. POISE introduces a curvature-aware critic regularization method that penalizes curvature-weighted greedy-action shift energy to reduce high-frequency action oscillations in actor-critic robotic control. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score by 5.9× on average, compared to 2.2× for the strongest baseline. High-frequency action oscillations degrade performance and safety in robotic control, and POISE offers a critic-side regularization that leaves the actor unchanged, potentially improving smoothness without sacrificing return. This could benefit practitioners using actor-critic methods in real-world robotics where smooth actions are critical. POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements using a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling. While it achieves the lowest smoothness score on five tasks, paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Actor-critic methods combine a policy (actor) and a value function (critic) to learn control tasks, but trained actors often produce jerky, high-frequency actions. Smoothness regularization typically constrains the actor, but recent work explores regularizing the critic to shape the policy indirectly. POISE builds on this by analyzing how the critic's preferred action shifts across states and penalizing the curvature-weighted energy of that shift.

## [QuirkyMind: Dual-Stream Refinement for Faithful LLM Persona Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31848) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.31848) introduces QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles persona identity definition from expression using a dual-stream latent state (sentence-level summary plus token-level sequence) refined with an alternating InfoNCE and cross-entropy objective. Evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference show it mitigates context drift while preserving authentic incongruities. This addresses a real tension in LLM personalization: prompting drifts over long contexts while fine-tuning tends to erase idiosyncratic traits in favor of generic patterns. If effective, the approach could enable more faithful, stable personas for role-play, companion agents, and personalized assistants. The method uses a discriminative InfoNCE loss to anchor the persona in representation space and a generative cross-entropy loss to ensure faithful verbalization, then transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. The paper is a cross-listing with no community discussion yet, so independent validation is pending.

**Background**: Persona steering aims to make LLMs consistently adopt a specified character or style. InfoNCE is a contrastive loss that pulls similar (anchor-positive) pairs together and pushes dissimilar (anchor-negative) pairs apart in embedding space, commonly used in representation learning. Dual-stream architectures process parallel data flows—here a sentence-level summary for semantic stability and a token-level sequence for generative control—to combine complementary information.

## [EEG-Jev: Unified Single-Pass Model for EEG Decision Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31875) ⭐️ 6.0/10

EEG-Jev is a unified single-pass decision model that, given an EEG window, a question, and an answer specification, returns typed readouts for choice, proposition, and score tasks. It was trained jointly on one checkpoint and evaluated on 35 public sources, achieving 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 pain ratings from ds005292. This work unifies diverse EEG analysis tasks into a single model with calibratable probabilities, potentially simplifying deployment and improving reliability in clinical and brain-computer interface applications. The reported calibration improvements and reduced latency make it relevant for real-time EEG-based systems. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and from 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) compared to a matched-backbone generative comparator. Performance is moderate overall, and the model is evaluated on held-out splits of public datasets rather than prospectively.

**Background**: EEG (electroencephalogram) records electrical brain activity and is widely used in neuroscience and clinical diagnostics. Traditional EEG analysis often trains separate models for different tasks such as motor imagery classification, sleep staging, and seizure detection. EEG-Jev proposes a single model that can handle multiple task types by conditioning on a question and answer specification, outputting calibrated probability distributions. A new arXiv paper (2611.31883) introduces Video-Relook, an experimental framework that lets multimodal models adaptively request temporal and spatial observations instead of relying on fixed frame sampling, and analyzes when these agentic harnesses improve video understanding. The authors report substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding and benefits extending to Video-MME-v2, but also find that gains vary widely across models and tasks, with some regressions. The work shifts attention from simply giving models the ability to request more observations to understanding whether they can use that ability reliably, which matters for designing agentic perception systems in video QA, robotics, and multimodal assistants. It suggests that adaptive observation policies must be matched to task demands and model capability rather than assumed to help universally. Using a common default observation configuration, the framework lets models revise their temporal and spatial observations, and interaction traces reveal differences in evidence seeking and answer-revision reliability across models. Benefits range from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions depending on the task, indicating that the observation interface alone does not guarantee effective use.

## [MIFLOW: Recency-Adaptive Flow Priors for Online Flow-Policy RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31902) ⭐️ 6.0/10

MIFLOW introduces a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions, using its approximate log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets in online flow-policy reinforcement learning. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, it achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than baselines on several tasks. This work addresses a key reliability issue in expressive flow-based policies: off-policy critics can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, causing policies to shift probability mass toward critic-favored but low-density actions. The proposed prior offers a lightweight regularization mechanism that could improve stability and final performance of flow-policy RL without discarding expressive action distributions. The correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available, and a Walker2d-v4 case study shows MIFLOW assigns a lower proportion of actions low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. However, true action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured, and prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and diagnostics.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Flow-based policies use flow matching, a generative modeling technique that learns continuous normalizing flows to represent complex action distributions, making them more expressive than Gaussian policies in continuous-control RL. Online actor-critic methods like SAC and TD3 rely on off-policy value estimates, which can be overestimated in regions with little data, and expressive policies may exploit these errors. MuJoCo is a standard physics simulator used by benchmarks such as Gym's continuous-control suite for evaluating RL algorithms.

A controlled diagnostic study evaluated InternVL3-2B on the DisasterM3 benchmark and found that using true pre/post image pairs yields only +0.5 accuracy points over a repeated-post control (95% CI [-0.2, +1.2]), indicating no measurable benefit from the pre-event image content. Reversing image order changed accuracy by only -0.2 points, showing little sensitivity to temporal order. This work highlights that lightweight vision-language models may answer change-related questions without truly relying on temporal evidence, which is critical for disaster assessment where comparing pre- and post-event scenes is essential. It argues that temporal benchmarks should report whether answers depend on the intended evidence, not just accuracy, impacting how the remote sensing community evaluates VLMs. The study used 1,659 optical and SAR image pairs from 41 events and nine disaster types in event-disjoint partitions, with 9,031 reasoning questions. While the model is not blind to the first image (true pair scores 2.5 points above an unrelated pre-event image), state-transition and multi-hop questions remain hard, and optical and SAR inputs show different profiles.

## [VIDE: Training-Free Video Anomaly Detection via Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32138) ⭐️ 6.0/10

VIDE is a training-free framework that adapts text-derived anomaly scoring to each test video using frozen CLIP embeddings, reducing anomaly bias and prompt sensitivity. It improves AUC over the best PRISM result by 1.5, 1.9, and 3.5 points on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, respectively, and AP by 6.5 points on XD-Violence and 9.3 points on MSAD. This work addresses key limitations of embedding-based video anomaly detection, such as anomaly bias and prompt sensitivity, without requiring additional training. It achieves state-of-the-art results among training-free methods on three benchmarks, which could make VAD more practical for real-world deployment where labeled data is scarce. VIDE estimates normal scene content from clips with low initial anomaly scores to partially correct the textual reference, rescales category responses, penalizes clips with strong responses across categories, and refines anomaly directions using high-scoring clips. It also averages scores across prompt views and fuses scores from two frozen encoders to reduce sensitivity to prompt selection.

## [Joint Classification and Generation on Tabular Data: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32225) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This arXiv paper empirically compares joint models that perform both classification and generation on tabular data, built from four model families—energy-based models, probabilistic circuits, tabular foundation models, and tabular diffusion models—across 29 datasets and measured FLOPs and wall-clock time. It finds that a probabilistic circuit is best at the smallest computational budgets, while beyond that a tabular foundation model (TabICL) that generates column by column using a regressor performs best. Practitioners often need both a classifier and a generator of realistic tabular records, and this study provides guidance on when a single joint model is a defensible alternative to training and maintaining two separate models. It shows joint models are rarely preferable but often very close to the best separate pair, which can simplify deployment and maintenance in tabular ML pipelines. The comparison uses two defined aggregate scores capturing different aspects of prediction and generation, and benchmarks against every pair of a separate classifier and generator at different computational budgets. The best joint model is a probabilistic circuit at the smallest budgets and TabICL beyond that, but a joint model is rarely preferable to the best separate pair, though often very close.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Tabular data—data organized in rows and columns, as in spreadsheets or databases—remains the most common format in applied machine learning. Many tasks require both predicting a target label (classification) and generating realistic synthetic records, traditionally done with two separate models. A joint model aims to provide both from one set of weights, and several tabular deep learning families can be adapted this way, including energy-based models, probabilistic circuits, tabular foundation models, and diffusion models such as TabDDPM.

## [CoMNO: Commutator Memory Neural Operator for Long-Horizon PDE Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32274) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a Commutator Memory Neural Operator (CoMNO) that identifies fine-scale dynamical details by commuting downsampling and rollout operations, and stores these details in a memory module to generate spatially adaptive corrections during rollout. Empirical results across five systems show improved prediction accuracy and long-horizon stability. This work addresses the critical problem of error accumulation in neural operators for long-horizon PDE prediction, which limits their practical use in scientific computing. The commutator-based approach offers a novel way to capture fine-scale features without sacrificing efficiency, potentially enabling more reliable long-term simulations in physics and engineering. The method exploits the performance gap between downsampling before rollout versus rollout before downsampling, where fine-scale details are encoded. A memory module stores these features along the trajectory and retrieves them to apply spatially adaptive corrections, enhancing fidelity over long horizons.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Neural operators are machine learning models that learn mappings between function spaces, providing efficient surrogates for solving PDEs compared to traditional numerical methods. However, when used for autoregressive rollout over long time horizons, they suffer from error accumulation because small inaccuracies at each step compound, often due to the failure to capture fine-scale dynamics. The commutator of two operations measures how much the order of applying them matters, and here it is used to quantify the information lost when downsampling is performed before prediction.

## [Research-Paper Context Can Hurt LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32381) ⭐️ 6.0/10

An exploratory Isaac Sim study found that providing an incremental-replanning research paper as context to Claude Opus 5 worsened the quadruped navigation controllers it wrote: when a maze's shortest route was blocked mid-episode, only 2 of 8 controllers written with the paper completed all four trips, versus 7 of 8 without it (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This counterintuitive result cautions against assuming that injecting research-paper context into LLM code generation always helps, and suggests that context can bias models toward paper-specific goals at the expense of the main task. It is relevant to anyone using LLMs to write robot controllers or other safety-critical code. The degradation appeared only under Isaac Sim physics; in an idealized kinematic simulator, controllers written with and without the paper were indistinguishable. The study is narrow—one LLM (Claude Opus 5), one robot (Unitree Go2), small samples (8 controllers per condition), and three code-generation settings (behavior trees, edited navigators, from-scratch controllers)—and the statistical evidence is modest.

## [Caption-Guided Loss Weights Audio-Visual Pairs by Semantic Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32399) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that uses modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video and weights positive pairs accordingly. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal, and applying CGAAL to three contrastive baselines consistently improves audio-visual retrieval performance. This work addresses a known limitation in audio-visual contrastive learning: not all paired samples are equally aligned, especially in unconstrained environments with off-screen sounds. By providing a general, model-agnostic weighting scheme, CGAAL can be integrated into existing contrastive frameworks to improve representation quality without architectural changes, potentially benefiting multimodal retrieval and related tasks. CGAAL leverages modality-specific captions to compute agreement scores that weight each positive pair, and it employs a warm-up period and gradual thresholding to avoid destabilizing early training. The method is evaluated on audio-visual retrieval across three contrastive baselines, showing consistent improvements, though the paper does not specify dataset details or computational overhead in the abstract.

**Background**: Multimodal contrastive learning is a self-supervised approach that aligns embeddings from different data types by contrasting paired and unpaired examples, typically assuming that paired observations provide shared views of the same information. Captions provide a way to estimate semantic content per modality, enabling more informed weighting of training pairs.

## [PHAR Framework Detects and Corrects Progress Hallucination in VLN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32400) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper identifies 'progress hallucination' as a failure mode in vision-and-language navigation (VLN) where agents misinterpret off-route observations as task progress, and proposes PHAR, a test-time verify-then-steer framework that uses VLM residual-stream representations and split conformal calibration to detect this mismatch and a contextual bandit to select rewind extent for recovery. This work addresses a specific and underexplored failure mode in VLN, potentially improving the reliability of embodied agents that follow natural language instructions in unseen 3D environments, which is relevant for robotics and multimodal AI systems. PHAR operates at test time without retraining, using residual-stream representations from a vision-language model to detect cross-modal evidence mismatch, with split conformal calibration to control false alarms, and a contextual bandit to adaptively choose how far to rewind instruction progress; experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show improved reliability for multiple state-of-the-art VLN methods.

Progress hallucination refers to the agent's internal estimate of instruction progress advancing incorrectly, which hampers recovery from route deviations. ## [BEACON: Learned Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Flow Matching in Microscopy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32406) ⭐️ 6.0/10

BEACON introduces a learned observation-conditioned coupling for guided conditional flow matching, replacing independent Gaussian noise with a lightweight conditional noise model that proposes K starting points per degraded input, selecting the one with lowest flow-matching loss during training. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the clean target. This work addresses a fundamental inefficiency in guided conditional flow matching for microscopy restoration, where arbitrary noise-target pairing produces conflicting velocity targets and hinders learning. By leveraging the degraded observation as a starting point, BEACON improves restoration quality across ten datasets and thirteen baseline families, potentially enabling cheaper and faster fluorescence imaging at lower light dose. BEACON achieves the best median perception-distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID) across ten microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution datasets. A KL term keeps the learned proposal close to the Gaussian prior, and code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Flow matching is a generative modeling paradigm that learns a continuous normalizing flow by regressing a velocity field that transports a simple base distribution (typically standard Gaussian noise) to the data distribution. Guided conditional flow matching extends this by incorporating a degraded observation into the conditional velocity field, and has shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution. However, standard training pairs each clean target with an independent Gaussian sample, so the starting point does not leverage the degraded observation, leading to conflicting velocity targets.

The paper introduces CaptionOPD, a caption-driven on-policy distillation method that replaces region-specific question-answer pairs with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts to provide broad visual supervision for fine-grained perception in vision-language models. Using only unlabeled images and region boxes, CaptionOPD outperforms prior on-policy distillation methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks. This work removes the costly and hard-to-scale QA curation bottleneck in multimodal on-policy distillation, enabling training on unlabeled images and broader supervision of visual elements within each region. CaptionOPD uses a fixed set of caption prompts ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout, and the model itself serves as the crop-view teacher, requiring no questions, answers, or larger model annotations—only images and region boxes. The method addresses three weaknesses of prior QA-based OPD: scalability limits, incomplete supervision of visual elements, and presupposition-induced hallucination.

## [PReS: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32474) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), a method for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B²-UniDA) that builds reliable target supervision without access to source data or source model parameters. PReS identifies reliable known samples using semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP, then adaptively integrates their predictions to construct pseudo labels. This work addresses a challenging and underexplored setting where adaptation must rely solely on black-box source model predictions, which are often unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. By combining foundation models like CLIP with diffusion-based perturbations, PReS offers a practical pathway for adapting models in privacy-sensitive or proprietary scenarios, potentially impacting fields where source data cannot be shared. PReS estimates sample-wise reliability of the black-box source model and CLIP, adaptively integrating their complementary predictions to form pseudo labels, and uses these asymmetrically to encourage confident predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the target-domain knowledge refines both pseudo labels and the known/unknown partition in a closed-loop process, and experiments show state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multiple benchmarks.

A new arXiv paper evaluates three classes of reinforcement learning algorithms—PPO (on-policy, model-free), SAC (off-policy, model-free), and Drama (model-based)—for their robustness to catastrophic forgetting in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment with four successively presented parking scenarios at varying angles. ## [ContinualDrive: A Deployment-Anchored Benchmark for Continual Learning of Driving Planners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32529) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ContinualDrive is a new benchmark for post-deployment continual learning of driving planners that updates a deployed planner on real-world nuPlan logs one scenario-type group at a time and evaluates the same checkpoints in both open and closed loop. It makes four measurement axes explicit—evaluation loop, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation, and stream protocol—and anchors a three-valued release verdict to the deployed checkpoint, showing that verdicts can reverse or vanish when an axis changes. This work exposes how unstated evaluation choices can flip release decisions for continually updated driving planners, which is critical for the autonomous driving and continual learning communities. It provides a reporting contract and will release code and all checkpoints, enabling more rigorous and reproducible evaluation of post-deployment updates. The study evaluates two planners (PlanTF and Diffusion Planner) under full fine-tuning and adapter or LoRA updates, with and without replay or gradient projection, across three task orders. Notably, open-loop ADE ranks the final PlanTF model above the deployed one in half of its core-suite runs, whereas every closed-loop score ranks it below; in the core suite, no regime measurably improved on the deployed planner in closed loop, and on a panel more than ten times larger every evaluated final checkpoint trails it.

## [Closed-Form Gradients Boost Deep Generative Scenario Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32573) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper derives closed-form gradients for Deep Generative Scenario Search (DGSS) using recourse duality and an adjoint solve, replacing the previous black-box gradient estimate. These analytical gradients are then integrated into a guided evolution strategy as a sampling subspace, rather than as a direct update. This provides a rigorous analytical foundation for decision-focused scenario generation in two-stage stochastic optimization, potentially leading to more efficient and accurate solutions for problems with integer variables. It bridges generative modeling with stochastic programming, impacting researchers and practitioners in operations research and machine learning. The decision-focused direction reduces the mean gap by three-quarters compared to the baseline, and on two families with the most integer variables, the reduced sets beat the exact solver's two-hour incumbent in most runs using only a fifth of the time. The guided evolution strategy ensures that even an inaccurate guide adds variance while the expected step still descends, as the expected update is a descent direction of the smoothed objective.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Two-stage stochastic programming is a framework for decision-making under uncertainty where first-stage decisions are made before uncertainty is revealed, and second-stage recourse decisions are made after. Deep Generative Scenario Search (DGSS) is a recent method that uses deep generative models to create synthetic scenarios and improves them by learning from the decisions they induce, but it originally relied on black-box gradient estimates because decisions are piecewise constant. This paper provides the missing analytical foundation by deriving gradients in closed form from recourse duality.

## [MSPO Separates Module-Specific Learning Signals in Multimodal RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32687) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules in multimodal reinforcement learning. MSPO uses responses to perception checklists to compute a Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR) for training the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. This work addresses module-level credit entanglement, a common limitation in GRPO-based training of MLLMs where all modules are optimized with the same advantage signal even when perceptual and final-answer correctness differ. By providing more targeted credit assignment, MSPO could improve multimodal reasoning performance and influence future RL fine-tuning methods for MLLMs. MSPO derives a vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR, scaled by main-task success rates, and uses a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. Experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks show that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both 3B and 7B scales.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically consist of a vision encoder, a projector, and a language model, and are trained with reinforcement learning to improve reasoning. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is an RL algorithm that fine-tunes LLMs using verifiable rewards, but in MLLMs it applies the same advantage to all modules, causing credit entanglement. MSPO aims to disentangle these signals by giving the vision encoder a perception-specific reward.

FourStat introduces a dual-model framework for univariate time series anomaly detection, combining a Fourier Autoencoder (FAE) that captures global seasonal patterns via frequency-domain analysis and a Stationary Autoencoder (SAE) that focuses on local structures by enforcing statistical stationarity. Most existing anomaly detection methods are designed for multivariate settings and perform poorly on univariate data, so FourStat addresses a gap by tailoring a dual approach to univariate series. The Perfect Point metric could reduce threshold-tuning bias in evaluations, offering a clearer comparison of model performance. The framework combines two complementary autoencoders: FAE leverages Fourier analysis to model global seasonality, while SAE enforces stationarity to capture local patterns. The Perfect Point metric eliminates the need for subjective threshold selection by checking if perfect F1-scores are achievable directly from anomaly scores.

Field Life is a new cellular automaton where each color is a chemical field, and an interaction matrix drives mass-conserving movement, yielding emergent gliders and structures. The authors release the simulation and 120 saved rules, called worlds, that produce moving patterns such as gliders and striped regions. This work bridges Particle Life and continuous cellular automata by introducing mass-conserving field dynamics, offering a new framework for studying emergent behavior in artificial life and complex systems. It could inspire new simulation models and provide a testbed for understanding how simple local rules generate structured movement. Each step involves convolving each color with a ring-shaped kernel to measure surrounding concentration, combining these via the interaction matrix into an attraction, and moving mass toward higher attraction while conserving mass. The authors sample random rules and keep those that move and form structure, describing patterns like color sorting, stripes, and gliders that break into smaller gliders.

This approach resolves the long-standing tension between scoring-based methods, which benefit from dense rewards but are limited to fixed action vocabularies, and anchor-based methods, which generate proposals dynamically but suffer from sparse supervision. ## [Transformer Inference Reinterpreted as Dynamic Parallel Processing via Output-Weight Interconnections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03921) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper presents a functionally equivalent mechanical-structural description of Transformer inference, identifying parameterized transformations of token representations with simple neural networks organized through output-input and output-weight interconnections. It introduces Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP) and shows that the number of dynamic parameters generated by a prompt grows linearly with prompt length, a phenomenon termed strong prompt sensitivity. This reinterpretation offers a novel theoretical lens on how Transformers process information, potentially impacting interpretability, control, and predictability of large language models. It also suggests connections to neuromorphic construction and biological language processing, which could inspire new architectures. The framework shows that outputs from the current input determine the weights of other networks, making inference a form of dynamic parallel processing. The linear growth of dynamic parameters with prompt length implies that longer prompts can make dynamic processing comparable to or exceed static processing, with implications for efficiency and interpretability.

**Background**: Transformers are the dominant architecture for large language models, typically described using matrix operations where weights are fixed after training. This paper proposes an alternative mechanical-structural view where some weights are dynamically generated during inference based on the input, akin to a network of networks. SIDPP is introduced as a conceptual framework to describe this dynamic processing, and strong prompt sensitivity highlights how the input prompt can significantly alter the effective computation.

## [Deep ReLU Regression Needs Only Linear Variation Budget for Quadratic Depth Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17434) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper establishes minimax risk lower bounds showing that deep ReLU regression can maintain statistical complexity quadratic in depth with a variation budget as small as O(L), far below the O(Lw^2) needed when each layer carries full gain. This result sharpens our theoretical understanding of how depth contributes to statistical complexity in deep ReLU networks, showing that a budget linear in depth already suffices for quadratic depth dependence, which could inform architecture design and regularization strategies. The analysis considers Gaussian regression on the circle over compositions of L vector-valued ReLU blocks of width w, with second-order variation costs summing to at most A; a budget CLw^ε forces minimax risk Ω(ε^2 min{1, L^2w^2 log w / n}) for each fixed ε∈(0,2] and L≳1/ε, and when L≳log w a budget CL forces risk Ω(min{1, L^2w^2/(n log w)}), while every function in the class has derivative variation at most 2(A/L)^L independent of width.

## [CaFE: A Refreshable, Capability-Focused Benchmark for Time Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26251) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose CaFE (Capability-Focused Evaluation), a refreshable evaluation extension that augments static time series foundation model benchmarks with structural diversity and multi-dimensional capability profiles. CaFE defines eight Structural Features (SFs), resamples original benchmark data according to each SF's structural support, removes edge-of-distribution samples, and augments retained samples by varying SF salience to produce a refreshed evaluation set. Experiments on GIFT-Eval and FEV-Mini20 show stable results and reveal per-feature strengths and weaknesses hidden by a single aggregate score. Static benchmarks with fixed test distributions encourage benchmark-specific tuning, so reported scores may reflect adaptation to the test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. CaFE makes model selection conditional on the structural response of interest, which could lead to more reliable model choices for practitioners and reduce leaderboard overfitting in the TSFM research community. CaFE retains conventional forecast-error metrics on the refreshed set and adds proposed intervention-response metrics, yielding a per-feature capability profile alongside endpoint accuracy. The authors report that on genuine data filtered by structural condition, models selected by CaFE outperform those chosen by the aggregate leaderboard.

The paper introduces Hadamard Transform-assisted multiplication-avoiding (HMA) operators that combine Walsh-Hadamard transform features with multiplication-avoiding channel mixing, and uses a gated formulation to identify which layers benefit from conventional multiplication. Experiments on ResNet-18 show that intermediate convolutional layers assign greater weight to HMA, while the earliest layers and final classifier retain more conventional computation. This work provides a practical path toward efficient compute-in-memory (CIM) inference by showing that Hadamard-domain feature restructuring can improve the accuracy-complexity tradeoff of multiplication-avoiding networks. It could enable more energy-efficient neural network deployment on specialized hardware. On CIFAR-10, the hybrid HMA ResNet-18 student achieves 91.2% accuracy (vs. 90.4% baseline) while reducing parameters by 68.25%, conventional MACs by 85.71%, and general multiplications by 85.54%. The approach matches or improves conventional models across ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet when combined with knowledge distillation.

The paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Industrial Vulnerability Index (AIIVI), a composite index built from fourteen concentration and sustainability parameters and aggregated using an O-Ring functional form, to assess potential production constraints in the foundation model industry. Applied to nine frontier developers as of August 31, 2026, it yields values of 0.75 under AI-elicited weights and 0.62 under equal weights, identifying compute and energy as the principal drivers of vulnerability. The index highlights that public investment may not target the most binding constraints, as it concentrates on compute while neglecting grid interconnection and generation. This matters for policymakers and industry stakeholders because it suggests a misalignment that could exacerbate supply chain vulnerabilities in the strategically important foundation model industry. The AIIVI is an index-based approximation derived from observable indicators and weighting assumptions, not a direct measurement of production constraints. The analysis also flags three underexamined exposures: increasing reliance on external debt for data-centre financing, local opposition as a constraint on data-centre siting, and export controls targeting deployed AI models rather than hardware.

On HotpotQA and OpenThoughts-TB-Dev, OP-Short surpasses the strongest BC baseline while cutting estimated teacher-inference cost by 20% and 83%, respectively; on ALFWorld, five-step continuations reduce teacher tokens by 22% versus full continuations with little accuracy loss. This work addresses a key weakness in generative segmentation—color drift and boundary mixing in rendered semantic RGB images—by providing a more robust decoding interface, which could improve reliability of segmentation models in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving. The hierarchical refinement and error-ranking method (C-IHD) also offer a way to quantify uncertainty without extra network passes, useful for deployment in adverse conditions. The generator uses a diffusion-distilled backbone with a single denoising update per crop, and interface logits are computed as distances to a fixed class-color codebook. HGEA combines multilevel VAE encoder features with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections, while C-IHD ranks pixel errors using pointwise uncertainty, local context, and refinement disagreement; on ACDC, C-IHD improves AUPR from 0.6580 to 0.7557 over max-softmax uncertainty.

**Background**: Generative segmentation methods use conditional image generators, often diffusion models, to produce semantic RGB images where each color corresponds to a class. Semantic Prism introduces an explicit interface that measures distances to a fixed color codebook and refines predictions hierarchically, leveraging features from the generator's VAE encoder.

## [Structural Coverage Analysis of Synthetic Priors in Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06912) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper reconstructs the synthetic data generators of four tabular foundation models (TFMs) and measures how well their pretraining priors structurally cover two widely used tabular benchmarks. Using structural descriptors for schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature-response relationships, the authors compute structural coverage and normalized density to quantify synthetic-to-benchmark support. This work offers a distribution-level attribution perspective on how synthetic pretraining data shapes downstream performance, which is important as TFMs like TabPFN and TabICL gain traction for tabular tasks. It suggests structural coverage can serve as a diagnostic for designing better synthetic priors, though the link to model behavior remains confounded with architecture and training. The analysis finds substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors, with some generators providing broader and denser support than others. Stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance, but this association is largely driven by the model with the broadest support and mostly disappears after removing each model's average support.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Tabular foundation models are pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, often using structural causal models, so they can perform in-context learning on new tabular datasets without task-specific training. However, it has been unclear how well these synthetic priors match the real-world benchmark datasets used for evaluation. This paper addresses that gap by reconstructing the generators and comparing their outputs to benchmark data using structural descriptors.

## [PointEvent: Polarity-Conditioned Recurrent Accumulation for Event-Based Tiny UAV Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20066) ⭐️ 6.0/10

PointEvent serializes event-camera streams into complementary spatiotemporal and timestamp orders, then uses polarity-routed recurrent state accumulation to connect sparse, fragmented target evidence across distant observations. It reports state-of-the-art accuracy on the EV-UAV and ES-UAV benchmarks with only 0.12M parameters and 29.9 ms inference time, with code released on GitHub. Tiny UAV detection is a core anti-drone capability where event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity, but distant targets produce weak, fragmented signals that dense aggregation tends to drown in clutter. PointEvent's lightweight design (0.12M parameters) and fast inference make it attractive for resource-constrained real-time edge deployment, and its polarity-conditioned propagation idea may generalize to other sparse event-based detection tasks. The method separates how evidence propagates (along serialized event paths) from where it is written (polarity-specific state subspaces), exploiting the fact that a moving target tends to produce opposite polarities at its leading and trailing boundaries. Evaluation is limited to the EV-UAV and ES-UAV benchmarks, and the 29.9 ms figure is a measured inference time rather than a guaranteed real-time bound across all hardware.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Event cameras are bio-inspired sensors that asynchronously report per-pixel brightness changes as events rather than producing intensity frames, giving them sub-millisecond temporal resolution and low latency. Each event carries a polarity indicating the sign of the brightness change, and a moving object typically triggers opposite polarities at its leading and trailing edges, which encodes motion direction. EV-UAV is a recent large-scale benchmark for event-based tiny UAV detection, where targets occupy very few pixels and events are sparse and noisy.

## [FlashReFocus: One Diffusion Pass for Fast Interactive Refocusing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23297) ⭐️ 6.0/10

FlashReFocus proposes running a diffusion model only once per photograph to restore an all-in-focus image, then using a lightweight renderer to produce each refocused edit. At 1536x1536 resolution, a complete refocus takes 2.45 seconds and each subsequent edit takes 0.46 seconds on a single RTX PRO 6000. This approach addresses the content instability and slow speed of generative refocusing methods that rerun large diffusion models for every edit, making interactive focal-plane comparison practical. It could benefit photographers and computational photography tools that need consistent, fast post-capture depth-of-field control. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and a defocus-bias attention mechanism to exchange information between tokens with similar blur magnitudes, enabling tilt-shift and two-plane effects. The authors also introduce 3CReal, an 89-pair benchmark from three camera-lens systems, and report leading fidelity and perceptual quality for zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Single-image refocusing aims to change the focal plane and depth of field of a photo after capture, typically by deblurring the image to an all-in-focus version and then re-blurring according to a chosen focus setting. Recent generative methods use diffusion models for this task, but rerunning them for every edit can cause inconsistent content changes and slow performance. FlashReFocus separates the ill-posed restoration step, which needs a generative prior, from the more deterministic blur-rendering step.

## [Endpoint-Calibrated Transport Enables One-Step Inversion-Free Image Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30827) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free image editing method that requires only a single noise-level evaluation. By exploiting a duality in variance-preserving (VP) one-step models, ECT derives a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement from one source-target query, then corrects the nominal transport via constrained projection. ECT eliminates the need for image inversion, trajectory integration, or iterative optimization, enabling extremely fast editing while maintaining quality. This could significantly lower the computational cost of real-image editing and make high-quality editing more accessible for practical applications. The method requires only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. It achieves stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time across reported benchmark settings.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Diffusion models for image editing typically rely on inversion—mapping a real image back to noise—followed by iterative sampling, which is slow and can introduce errors. One-step editors aim to speed this up but often need multiple noise-level evaluations to stabilize large updates. Variance-preserving (VP) models are a class of diffusion models that maintain unit variance throughout the process, and ECT leverages their analytical properties to avoid inversion entirely.

## [TRACE-CBM: Editable Concept States for Video Activity Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00020) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution) is a new concept bottleneck model that forecasts future video activities by recursively predicting editable, human-understandable concept states over time. It refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs and supports inference-time editing of concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates. This work extends concept bottleneck models from static prediction to temporal forecasting, making the intermediate reasoning of activity forecasting inspectable and steerable. It could improve trust and human-AI collaboration in applications like surveillance, robotics, and assistive systems where understanding and correcting forecasts is critical. TRACE-CBM conditions each concept transition on the prior activity distribution and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. Experiments show it improves observed-activity accuracy over concept-based methods and stays close to black-box forecasters, while concept edits correct some incorrect forecasts without flipping correct ones.

**Background**: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) are interpretable architectures that first map inputs to a set of human-understandable concepts, then use those concepts for prediction, allowing inspection and editing of intermediate states. Video activity forecasting involves predicting future actions or events from ongoing video, which requires modeling how objects, actions, and their interactions evolve over time. Spatio-temporal graphs are often used to represent such relational dynamics in video understanding.

## [Lightweight Evaluation Preserves Trajectory for Low Tucker Rank Tensor Estimators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01168) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a trajectory-preserving lightweight evaluation for iterative low Tucker rank tensor estimators, showing that three known components can reduce memory usage without altering the iteration trajectory. It formalizes exactness as an intertwining relation and demonstrates that computing only needed singular triplets, contracting without Kronecker products, and storing sparse-plus-factored states satisfy this relation for five estimators. This work addresses memory as the limiting resource for large tensors and edge devices, enabling exact implementations of methods like HOOI to run on hardware with limited memory. It provides a formal condition for when rewritings keep iterates unchanged, which could guide efficient implementations in tensor decomposition libraries. On an A100 GPU, lightweight HOOI uses 95× less memory beyond the input than the lightest exact implementation on 800³ tensors and is the fastest method reaching the HOOI estimate on the largest tensors. Against efficient public code, it is faster and lighter for three of five estimators, and it is the only implementation that fits a 1 GiB and a 4 GiB device for surveillance video and satellite hyperspectral cube data, respectively.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: Low Tucker rank tensor estimation is a technique for approximating high-dimensional arrays by exploiting low-rank structure, commonly used in signal processing and machine learning. Iterative methods like HOOI (Higher-Order Orthogonal Iteration) repeatedly compute large intermediate objects such as unfoldings, Kronecker operators, and full SVDs, which consume significant memory. This paper shows how to avoid these costs while preserving the exact same iterates and convergence guarantees.

## [MADJEPA: Multi-Stage JEPA for Medical Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25194) ⭐️ 6.0/10

MADJEPA introduces a multi-stage training pipeline built on the Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) for medical anomaly detection using only healthy images. The pipeline combines I-JEPA pretraining, target encoder distillation to curb over-generalization to abnormal data, and pseudo-anomaly classification to tighten the normal-data boundary, ranking first on three of six medical imaging datasets. This work shows that world-model-style self-supervised learning, previously demonstrated mainly on natural images and video, can be adapted to the label-scarce medical imaging domain. It offers a competitive alternative for unsupervised anomaly detection in MRI, OCT, X-ray, and histopathology, where annotated abnormalities are expensive to obtain. Ablation studies show that I-JEPA alone is insufficient for competitive medical anomaly detection, confirming that the distillation and pseudo-anomaly stages are essential. The code is publicly released on GitHub, and the method is evaluated across six datasets spanning multiple imaging modalities.

**Background**: JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) is a self-supervised framework that learns by predicting abstract representations of inputs rather than reconstructing raw pixels. I-JEPA, introduced by Meta AI in 2023, applies this idea to images by predicting representations of target blocks from a context block within the same image. Medical anomaly detection typically trains only on healthy patient data, since labeled abnormalities are scarce, and then flags deviations from the learned model of normality.

## [Counterfactual Supervision Teaches 3D-Aware Editors When to Trust Geometry vs. Photos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29542) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes counterfactual state supervision, which creates controlled photo–state conflicts via hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows/reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement, to train a 3D-aware object editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. It also introduces symmetric counterfactual correction, using state-side and photo-side twins to construct directed latent perturbations and train recovery, ensuring the learned distinction is maintained during sampling without architectural changes or extra inference steps. This work addresses a key ambiguity in 3D-aware object editing: when reconstructed 3D geometry conflicts with the photograph, the editor must decide which source to trust. By teaching this source-selection explicitly during training, the method improves spatial editing performance and content preservation, potentially benefiting applications in image manipulation, AR/VR, and content creation. Both strategies operate only during training and require no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench show strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, with controlled ablations indicating improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 26, 05:00

**Background**: 3D-aware object editing involves rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph, which requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets rendered at the target pose provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph. Standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust when such conflicts arise.
